ranges.en: Megillah is read on Adar 11 through 15, never earlier and never later.
Walled cities from Joshua's days read on the fifteenth.
Villages and large towns read on the fourteenth as the default.
Exception: villages may move the reading earlier to the day of gathering.
Asks how the rule works when the fourteenth falls on a given weekday.
If the fourteenth is Monday, villages and large towns read that day; walled cities read the next day.
If Tuesday or Wednesday, villages shift to gathering day, large towns read that day, walled cities the next.
If Thursday, villages and large towns read that day; walled cities read the next day.
If Friday, villages shift to gathering day; large towns and walled cities read that day.
If Shabbat, villages and large towns shift to gathering day; walled cities read the next day.
If Sunday, villages shift to gathering day, large towns read that day, walled cities the day after.
Restates that the Megillah is first read on the eleventh of Adar.
Asks from where the source for the multi-day reading is derived.
Explains the leniency: villages move reading earlier so they can supply food and water to walled cities.
Argues all these dates must be Great Assembly enactments, since later courts could not have overturned them.
Cites the Mishnah that one court cannot annul another's ruling unless greater in wisdom and number.
Concludes that the Men of the Great Assembly enacted all of these days.
Asks where in Scripture this enactment is hinted.
Introduces R. Yohanan's answer, transmitted through Rav Shemen b. Abba.
Cites Esther 9:31 to uphold keeping the Purim days in their appointed times.
Explains that 'their times' means the Sages established many times for them.
Asks whether the verse's wording is needed for its literal sense; if so, why not say 'time'?
Glosses 'their times' as indicating many times.
Asks whether the plural is needed to show one's time differs from another's.
If so, why not say 'their time'; why the plural 'their times'?
Concludes the plural teaches that all of these are to be inferred from it.
Proposes that 'all of them' simply means many times, rejecting the prior inference.
Argues 'their times' parallels 'their time': as 'time' means two days, 'times' means two more.
Asks why not read the twelfth and thirteenth instead.
R. Shmuel b. Yitzchak: the thirteenth is an assembly day needing no extra indication; the same applies here.
Asks why not the sixteenth and seventeenth instead.
Cites Esther 9:27, 'it shall not pass', to exclude the sixteenth and seventeenth.
Introduces R. Shmuel b. Nahmani's derivation from Scripture.
Cites Esther 9:22, 'as the days', which includes the eleventh and twelfth.
Explains that 'as the days' includes the eleventh and twelfth.
Asks why not the twelfth and thirteenth instead.
R. Shmuel b. Yitzchak's reply: the thirteenth is an assembly day, needing no extra textual indication.
Asks why not the sixteenth and seventeenth.
Cites 'it shall not pass' to exclude the sixteenth and seventeenth.
Asks why R. Shmuel b. Nahmani did not derive the rule from 'in their times'.
He does not accept the distinction between 'time', 'their time', and 'their times'.
Asks why R. Shemen b. Abba did not derive the rule from 'as the days'.
Explains that the phrase is meant to apply to future generations.
R. Yohanan's teaching: this is R. Akiva's view, who distinguishes 'time', 'their time', and 'their times'.
The Sages hold the Megillah is read only on its proper day.
Objection from a baraita of R. Judah: today the Megillah is read only on its proper day, since the calendar is fixed.
Asks whose opinion R. Judah follows: R. Akiva's or the Rabbis'.
If R. Akiva, the rule would apply even today; so it must be the Rabbis, who still read on other days.
This refutes R. Yohanan's position.
Offers an alternative transmission: Rabbah b. bar Hana in R. Yohanan's name, with the same attribution.
Reconciles: R. Akiva's view applies, while the Sages hold that today, since people reckon by it, it is read only on its proper day.
A baraita of R. Judah supports the reconciled reading.
R. Ashi notes a contradiction between two of R. Judah's statements.

ranges.en: Resolves the contradicting baraita by ascribing it to R. Yose b. R. Judah.
Challenges: could R. Judah really hold that today the Megillah is read only on its proper day?
Objection from a baraita of R. Judah: where travel to town occurs Monday and Thursday, reading shifts; elsewhere it stays on the proper day.
Maintains that where people do travel on those days, the earlier reading still applies today; the baraita follows R. Yose b. R. Judah.
Explains that the resolution was chosen because R. Judah appeared to contradict himself.
R. Ashi heard that some transmit the baraita as R. Judah's and others as R. Yose b. R. Judah's.
Concludes the R. Judah attribution is imprecise and the R. Yose b. R. Judah attribution is the accurate one.
Walled cities from Joshua b. Nun's days read on the fifteenth.
Asks from where this rule is derived.
Rava cites Esther 9:19: villages read on the fourteenth, so walled towns read on the fifteenth.
Objects: why not have villages read on the fourteenth and walled towns not at all? Israelites live there too.
Proposes that walled towns read on both the fourteenth and fifteenth, with villages on the fourteenth.
Cites Esther 9:21 'the fourteenth and the fifteenth' as the textual basis for the proposal.
Refutes the proposal: the particle 'et' separates the two days, assigning one to each group.
Proposes walled cities may choose either the fourteenth or the fifteenth.
Scripture's 'their times' shows one group's time is not the same as another's.
Proposes the thirteenth, as in Shushan.
Shushan's custom establishes that both celebration and remembrance are involved.
Asks how we know that the reading must occur on these days.
Cites Esther 9:28: 'remembering' is compared to 'keeping', so the reading is tied to the festival days.
Counter-baraita: R. Joshua b. Korha says cities walled since Ahasuerus's days read on the fifteenth, against our Mishnah.
Asks the reason for R. Joshua b. Korha's ruling.
Just as Shushan, walled since Ahasuerus's days, reads on the fifteenth, so do all such cities.
Asks the reason for our Tanna's ruling.
Analogy of 'villagers' with 'unwalled towns' in Deuteronomy 3:5 shows the cutoff is Joshua b. Nun's days.
Asks why our Tanna rejects R. Joshua b. Korha's view, given the same analogy he accepts.
R. Joshua b. Korha rejects the analogy because he does not draw it from 'villagers' to 'villagers'.
Asks which rule Shushan followed, since it was neither villages nor walled towns.
Rava's explanation: Shushan is an exception because a miracle occurred there.
On our Tanna's view, 'city and city' and 'town and town' in Esther 9:28 distinguish the two walled periods.
R. Joshua b. Korha's approach: 'city and city' distinguishes Shushan from other towns.
If so, asks what 'town and town' serves to teach.
Counter: is our Tanna's reading reasonable, given that he already has villages and towns separated?
The verse's wording is there for a midrashic derivation, not a separate rule.
R. Joshua b. Levi's rule: a city, its adjoining areas, and what the eye takes in with it count as a city.
Asks how far the adjoining area extends.
R. Jeremiah (or R. Hiyya b. Abba): up to a mil, measured from Hamtan to Tiberias.
R. Jeremiah (or R. Hiyya b. Abba) states that the letter forms were prescribed by the Watchmen.
Objects: Scripture says 'these are the commandments', which implies no prophet may add anything new.
Cites Leviticus 27:34: no prophet may introduce new matters, supporting the objection.
Cites R. Hisda: the mem and samekh in the Tablets were a case of fixed form, against later additions.

ranges.en: The letters remained in place by a miracle.
Explains the letter forms: people were unsure, so the Watchmen fixed open forms medially and closed forms finally.
Objects: the verse 'these are the commandments' implies no prophet may add anything new later.
Replies that the laws were forgotten and later re-established, not newly added.
Attributes the Targum of the Torah to Onkelos under R. Eliezer and R. Joshua, and the Targum of the Prophets to Jonathan b. Uzziel under Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi.
When the Prophets' Targum was published the land quaked, and a Heavenly Voice asked who revealed the secrets.
Jonathan answers that he did it for God's honor, to prevent disputes in Israel.
Jonathan then sought to render the Writings; a Heavenly Voice stopped him.
Asks the reason for the Heavenly Voice's prohibition.
Because the date of the Messiah is foretold in the Writings.
Asks whether Onkelos the convert really composed the Targum of the Torah.
Objects with Rav's teaching, transmitted through R. Ika, which seems to conflict with that attribution.
Interprets Nehemiah 8:8 as referring to the text, the Targum, the sense, and the accents.
Alternative reading: the phrase refers to the Masorah, which was forgotten and reestablished.
Asks why the land quaked over the Prophets' translation but not over the Torah's.
The Torah's meaning is plain, while the Prophets' meaning is partly plain and partly obscure.
Cites Zechariah 12:11 on the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddo as an obscure prophetic passage.
R. Joseph: without the Targum of this verse we would not understand its meaning.
Gives the Aramaic Targum, comparing the mourning to that for Ahab and for Josiah.
Cites Daniel 10:7: Daniel alone saw the vision, while the men with him fled in fear.
Asks who the men with Daniel were.
R. Jeremiah (or R. Hiyya b. Abba): they were Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi.
They surpassed him as prophets; he surpassed them because he alone saw the vision.
Asks why they were frightened if they did not see the vision.
Though they did not see, their star saw, so they were frightened.
Ravina: one frightened though seeing nothing is affected because his star sees.
Ravina's remedies: recite the Shema, move four cubits away from foulness, or recite the goat-at-the-butcher's formula.
Asks the purpose of 'family and family' if 'city and city' and 'town and town' already serve a derashah.
R. Yose b. Hanina: the families of priests and Levites stop their service to come hear the Megillah.
R. Judah in Rav's name: priests, Levites and Israelites all stop their service to hear the Megillah.
A baraita teaches the same: priests, Levites and Israelites all stop their service to hear the Megillah.
From this, the House of Rabbi concluded that Torah study may also be interrupted to hear the Megillah.
A fortiori argument: if Temple service may be suspended, Torah study may be suspended all the more.
Objects to the a fortiori: Joshua prostrated before a man at Jericho, so service is not always weightier.
Asks how Joshua could greet a figure at night, since greeting at night is forbidden for fear of demons.
It was different there: the figure announced he was captain of the Lord's host.
Objects: perhaps the figure was lying; but we learned that God's name is not uttered in vain.
The figure rebukes Joshua for neglecting the evening daily offering and now his Torah study.
Joshua asks for which of the two obligations the figure came.
The figure replies that he has come now, for the present matter.
Cites Joshua 8:9: Joshua spent that night in the midst of the valley.
Introduces the following teaching by attributing it to R. Yohanan.

ranges.en: Teaches that Joshua spent the night immersed in the depths of halakhah.
R. Shmuel b. Unia: Torah study outweighs the daily offerings.
Cites Joshua's words 'I have come now' as the basis for that claim.
No contradiction: one statement concerns the whole people's study, the other an individual's.
Mishnah on festival mourning, with exceptions for Hanukkah and Purim, challenges the lesser value of individual study.
Rabbah b. Huna: a festival bars mourning customs in a scholar's presence, all the more on Hanukkah and Purim.
Replies that this concerns honoring Torah, while an individual's study ranks lower.
Rava: reading the Megillah outweighs Temple service and Torah study, following R. Yose b. Hanina and the House of Rabbi.
Rava: attending to a met mitzvah outweighs Torah study and Temple service, as a baraita on neglecting study shows.
Cites Numbers 6:7, 'or for his sister', to bound the rule of defilement.
A baraita derives from 'or for his sister' that one may defile himself for a met mitzvah but not for a relative.
Rava asks whether reading the Megillah or attending to a met mitzvah takes precedence, and on what ground.
Rava's answer: the met mitzvah takes precedence, because of the respect owed to people.
Cites the teaching that respect for people overrides a biblical negative precept.
R. Joshua b. Levi defines a city to include adjacent and visible areas.
A baraita: adjoining areas count even if not visible, and visible areas count even if not adjoining.
Asks how a case of adjoining but not visible areas could arise.
R. Jeremiah: a city situated in a valley produces that case.
R. Joshua b. Levi: a city settled first and walled later is reckoned as a village.
Asks the reason for that ruling.
Leviticus 25:29, 'walled city', shows the city must have been walled first and then settled.
R. Joshua b. Levi: a city without ten men of leisure is reckoned as a village.
Asks what new point this teaches, since it seems already known.
Mishnah: a large town has ten men of leisure; fewer makes it a village.
The point is needed to show the rule holds even when outsiders come to the city.
R. Joshua b. Levi: a city laid waste and later resettled is reckoned as a city.
Asks what 'laid waste' means: walls destroyed, or the city later resettled?
Objects with a baraita of R. Eliezer b. Yose: a walled city counts even if it has no wall now, if it once had one.
Resolves: 'laid waste' means it has lost its ten men of leisure.
Introduces a further ruling of R. Joshua b. Levi, cut off at the end of the daf.

ranges.en: Lod, Ono and Gei Haharashim were walled since the days of Joshua b. Nun.
Objects: was it Joshua who built these towns, or was it Elpaal?
Cites 1 Chronicles 8:12: Elpaal's sons built Ono and Lod with their surrounding towns.
Counters that Asa built them, citing 2 Chronicles 14:5 on the fortified cities of Judah.
R. Elazar: these places were walled since the days of Joshua b. Nun.
They were ruined in the days of the Gibeah concubine, rebuilt by Elpaal, fell again, and were repaired by Asa.
2 Chronicles 14:6, 'let us build these cities', indicates they were already towns beforehand.
Concludes from the verse that these places were towns from the outset.
Joshua b. Levi: women are obligated to read the Megillah, since they too were part of the miracle.
Joshua b. Levi: if Purim falls on Shabbat, one asks questions and offers derashot on that day's subject.
Asks why Purim is singled out, since the same rule applies to festivals.
Baraita: Moses instituted topical questions and derashot for each festival, so the rule covers all festivals.
Purim needed explicit mention, lest it be forbidden out of concern over Rabbah's rule.
Joshua b. Levi: one must read the Megillah at night and repeat it by day.
Cites Psalms 22:3, 'I cry in the daytime... and in the night', as support for the repetition.
R. Jeremiah: 'repeat' means review, as one goes over a section of study, following R. Hiyya b. Abba.
R. Helbo in Ulla's name: one must read the Megillah at night and repeat it by day.
Cites Psalms 30:13 in support of repeating the reading by day.
Villages may move the reading forward to the day of gathering.
R. Hanina: the Sages were lenient so villagers could supply food and water to their brothers in the walled cities.

ranges.en: Glosses that the enactment was made for the benefit of the walled cities.
Objects from a Mishnah: if it falls on Monday, shifting to the prior day would require a tenth day, which the Sages never fixed.
Objects from a Thursday case: the day of gathering cannot be shifted to another day.
Objects with R. Judah's baraita: if cities are not visited on Monday and Thursday, the enactment would harm them.
Corrects the rationale: villagers shift the reading because they supply food and water to their brothers in the walled cities.
Mishnah illustration: when the fourteenth falls on Monday or Shabbat, villages and large towns read on that day.
Asks why the first case gives dates of the month while the second gives days of the week.
Because reversing the dates would be awkward, the Mishnah switches to giving the days of the week.
Mishnah case: the fourteenth falls on Friday.
Asks which authority the Mishnah follows: Rabbi or R. Yose.
Baraita on a Friday fourteenth: the first view shifts villages; Rabbi holds that neither group shifts and both read that day.
Asks the reason for the first Tanna's view.
Derives from 'every year': as towns read before walled cities each year, so here.
Counter-analogy from 'every year' that towns need not shift; distinguishes this case as one that cannot be avoided.
Asks Rabbi's reason.
From 'every year': towns need not shift, as in most years, so here they need not shift either.
Counter-analogy: towns read before walled cities in most years, so they should here; distinguished as unavoidable.
Asks the source of R. Yose's view.
Baraita of R. Yose: on a Friday, walled cities do not precede towns; both groups read on the day itself.
Asks the reason for the first Tanna's view.
From 'every year': towns read on the fourteenth, and one group's time differs from another's, so here too.
Counter-analogy: walled cities need not precede towns; distinguished as unavoidable.
Asks R. Yose's reason.
From 'every year': walled cities do not precede towns in most years, so they should not here.
Counter-analogy: each year's times differ, so here too; distinguished as unavoidable.
Asks whether Rabbi really held that towns should not shift to the day of gathering.
Baraita with Shabbat: villages shift; Rabbi says that since towns already shift, they may shift to the day of gathering.
Distinguishes: Shabbat is the proper day there, so shifting further is allowed; here the proper day is Friday.
Asks whose opinion this follows.
R. Helbo in R. Huna's name: if Purim falls on Shabbat, all shift their reading to the day of gathering.
Objects: not all shift, since walled cities read on Sunday.
Rather, all who shift shift to the day of gathering, which follows Rabbi's view.
All agree the Megillah is not read on Shabbat.
Asks the reason.
Rabbah: all are obligated, but not all are skilled readers; a decree prevents carrying the scroll four cubits in a public domain.
The same reasoning applies to the shofar and the lulav on Shabbat.
Rav Yosef: the poor eagerly await the reading of the Megillah, which is the reason.
Baraita: although villages shift to the day of gathering, contributions are collected and distributed that same day.
Objects: 'although they said' should be read as 'on the contrary, it is because they said'.
Resolves the wording: since villages shift, collections happen that day, because the poor await the Megillah reading.

ranges.en: Rejoicing of Purim is observed only at its proper time.
Rav holds that a Megillah read at its proper time may be read even by an individual.
Rav Asi holds that reading outside the proper time requires a quorum of ten, with both timings compared.
A case occurred, and Rav took Rav Asi's view into account.
Challenge: did Rav really say this?
Objection citing Rav's teaching that when Purim falls on Shabbat, Friday is the proper time.
Objection: Shabbat itself is surely the proper time.
Reply: rather, Rav meant something different.
Reply: the alternative time has the same status as the proper time for individual reading.
Reply: Rav's rule about ten applies to reading the Megillah itself.
Asks what is meant by Friday being the proper time.
Answer: Rav rejects Rabbi's view, so Friday is the proper day to shift to.
Mishnah defines a large town as one with ten idle men; fewer makes it a village.
Mishnah: these observances are moved earlier but not postponed.
Mishnah: wood-bringing, Tisha B'Av, hagigah and assembly are postponed, not moved earlier.
Mishnah: despite moving earlier, mourning, fasting and gifts to the poor are permitted.
Rabbi Judah: the rule depends on whether a place gathers on Mondays and Thursdays.
Baraita: the ten men of leisure are those in the synagogue.
Restatement: these observances are moved earlier but not postponed.
Asks for the reason.
Abba, in Shmuel's name, gives the reason.
Scripture verse 'and it shall not pass' is cited as support.
R. Abba, in Shmuel's name, adds a second teaching.
Asks how we know years are not counted by days.
Exodus verse about months of the year implies reckoning years by months, not days.
Rabbis of Caesarea, in R. Abba's name, teach a parallel point.
Asks how we know months are not reckoned by hours.
Numbers verse about a month of days implies reckoning months by days, not hours.
Restatement of the Mishnah: these are postponed and not moved earlier.
Reasons: Tisha B'Av hastens no punishment, and hagigah's obligation has not yet arrived.
Baraita: the festival sacrifice and its whole period are postponed.
Asks what the period of the festival sacrifice means.
R. Oshaya explains the festival sacrifice is postponed when the festival falls on Shabbat.
Asks whose view this is.
Mishnah of Beth Shammai and Beth Hillel on bringing festival offerings is cited.
Rava: the festival sacrifice may be postponed for the whole festival period, but no further.
Mishnah cited: one who missed the festival sacrifice may bring it during the festival, with no later compensation.
R. Ashi: the festival sacrifice may be postponed through the festival period, even for Shavuot.
Mishnah cited: Beth Hillel agree that when Shavuot falls on Shabbat, slaughter is after Shabbat.
R. Elazar, in R. Hanina's name, reports that Rabbi planted a sapling on Purim.

ranges.en: Narrative: Rabbi bathed in Tzippori on the 17th of Tammuz and tried to abolish the Tisha B'Av fast, but his colleagues refused.
Abba b. Zavda objects that this was not what happened.
Correct account: Tisha B'Av fell on Shabbat and was postponed until after Shabbat.
Rabbi argued that since it was postponed, it should be postponed altogether, but the Sages disagreed.
Rabbi cites the Ecclesiastes verse that two are better than one as a supporting argument.
Asks how Rabbi could have planted a sapling on Purim.
Baraita of R. Joseph: Purim's rejoicing, feasting and good day forbid mourning, fasting and work.
Rabbi was from a place that observed Purim on the 14th, and he planted on the 15th.
Objection: Rabbi lived in Tiberias, which was walled since Joshua's time.
Rabbi was from a place keeping Purim on the 15th, and he planted on the 14th.
Objection: Hezekiah read in Tiberias on both days, so the walled status was doubtful to him.
Asks whether Rabbi was truly certain about Tiberias.
Objection: Megillat Ta'anit forbids mourning on the 14th and 15th, so this could not be permitted.
Rava replies that the mention of those days only extends forbiddance across the two days.
Rava limits this to mourning and fasting; work is forbidden only on one day.
Objection: Rav cursed a man who planted flax on Purim, which contradicts Rava's limit.
Rabbah son of Rava: the people accepted mourning and fasting on those days, but not work.
Esther verses: the first mention includes good day, the later one omits it, supporting the limit.
Asks why Rav cursed that man.
Permitted things that others made a custom of abstaining from; that was not the custom in Rabbi's place.
Alternatively, the custom was observed, and Rabbi planted a festive sapling.
Mishnah cited: those days lessen business, building, planting, betrothal and marriage.
Baraita: building and planting here mean festive building and festive planting.
Asks what festive building is.
Festive building is one who builds a wedding house for his son.
Asks what festive planting is.
Festive planting is one who plants a royal abarnaki tree.
Restating the text: Hezekiah read on both days, doubtful whether Tiberias was walled since Joshua.
Objection: how could he doubt Tiberias, given the verse listing Rakat among fortified cities?
Joshua verse lists the fortified cities, including Rakat and Kinnereth.
It is established that Rakat is Tiberias.
Reason for the doubt: one side of Tiberias is bounded by the lake, which is a natural barrier.
If so, why was he still in doubt?
A lake shore is certainly not a wall.
Leviticus verse: a walled city has a wall, not a fence of houses, and Tiberias is excluded because the sea is its wall.
Hezekiah was not in doubt about the houses of a walled town, but about the Megillah reading rule.
Asks what distinguishes villages from walled towns for Megillah reading, given the two possible rationales.
Rav Assi read in Huzal on both days; some report Rav Assi said Huzal of Benjamin was walled since Joshua.
R. Yohanan recounts that as a boy he asked the elders about something he had said.
