ranges.en: Identifies Hamat as Tiberias, as previously argued.
Asks why Hamat is so named.
Named for the hot springs of Tiberias.
Identifies Rakat as Tzippori.
Asks why Rakat is so named.
Named because it slopes like the bank of a river.
Identifies Kinnereth as Ginosar.
Asks why Kinnereth is so named.
Named because its fruit is sweet like the sound of a harp.
Rava challenges anyone who would deny that Rakat is Tiberias.
Mourning customs in Babylonia and Tiberias show Rakat refers to Tiberias.
A eulogy for R. Zera calls the mourned place Rakat, again identifying it with Tiberias.
Rabbah gives an alternative account of the identifications.
Rabbah identifies Hamat with Gerar's hot springs, Rakat with Tiberias, and Kinnereth with Ginosar.
Asks why Rakat is so named.
Its least worthy inhabitants are still full of mitzvot, like a pomegranate.
R. Jeremiah holds that Rakat is simply its name.
Asks why Tiberias is so named.
Tiberias lies at the center of the land of Israel.
Rava holds that Rakat is its name.
Asks why Tiberias is so named.
Its appearance is good, hence Tiberias.
Zeira identifies Kitron with Tzippori.
Asks why Tzippori is so named.
Tzippori sits on a mountaintop like a bird (tzippor).
Objection: Kitron was in the territory of Zevulun, so it cannot be Tzippori.
Judges verse shows Zevulun failed to drive out Kitron's inhabitants and complained about his portion.
Judges verse shows Zevulun was a people risking its life.
Asks what the reason for Zevulun's complaint is.
Because Naphtali received the high places of the field.
Zevulun complains to God that his brothers received fields and vineyards while he received hills and seas.
God replies that all of them need Zevulun for the hilazon snail.
Deuteronomy verse about peoples calling to the mountain supports God's answer.
R. Joseph taught the hidden treasures are the hilazon, the tunny fish, and white glass.
Zevulun asks who will inform him of this.
God answers with the verse about offering righteous sacrifices.
God's sign: whoever takes from Zevulun without payment will not profit in his business.
If Kitron were Tzippori, Zevulun's complaint would make no sense.
Tzippori is a far better place, so it would not lack milk and honey.
Resh Lakish testifies that he saw milk and honey flowing around Tzippori.
Tzippori measures sixteen by sixteen miles.
Objection: Zevulun's portion may still be inferior to his brothers'.
Rabbah b. Bar Hanah cites R. Yohanan's testimony.
R. Yohanan says he saw milk and honey throughout the land of Israel.
The land of Israel extends about twenty-two parasangs in length and six in breadth.
Even so, Zevulun preferred fields and vineyards.
Judges verse about Naphtali on the high places of the field shows the same preference.
The conclusion is drawn from this verse.
R. Abbahu cites Zephaniah: Ekron shall be uprooted.
Ekron is Caesarea, the daughter of Edom, sitting among the sands.
Caesarea was a thorn in Israel's side under the Greeks until the Hasmoneans conquered it.
The conquest was called the capture of the tower of Shir.
R. Yose b. Hanina introduces an interpretation of a verse.
Asks what the cited verse means.
Zechariah verse about removing blood and detestable things from the mouth.
The verse's parts are read as referring to Edom's shrines, oracles, synagogues and study houses.
Zechariah verse about a chieftain in Judah.
Ekron as a Jebusite refers to Edom's theatres and circuses, where Judah will teach Torah publicly.
R. Yitzchak introduces his teaching on Ekron.
A verse about Ekron being uprooted is cited.
Caesarea, daughter of Edom, was a metropolis of kings.
Two opinions: kings were brought up there, or kings were appointed from there.
Caesarea and Jerusalem are rivals; if one is destroyed, the other flourishes, so do not believe reports of both alike.
Ezekiel verse 'I shall be filled, she is laid waste' supports the rivalry principle.
R. Nahman b. Yitzchak derives the same lesson from Genesis about two nations.
R. Yitzchak asks what the verse about the wicked means.
Isaiah verse: the wicked, Yohan, does not learn righteousness.
Isaac pleads before God for mercy on Esau.
God replies that Esau is wicked.
Isaac objects that Esau has not learned righteousness.
God replies with the verse that Esau deals wrongfully in the land of uprightness.
Isaac replies that then Esau should not see God's majesty.
R. Yitzchak introduces a second teaching.
Asks what the verse in Psalms means.
Psalm verse: do not grant the wicked's desires or further his plot.
Jacob prays before God that Esau's desire and plot not be granted.

6b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Germania of Edom: if its people went forth they would destroy the entire world.
R. Hama b. Hanina: Germania has 300 crowned heads, Rome has 365 chieftains, and they constantly fight.
R. Yitzchak's principle: a claim of toil without success or success without toil is not to be believed; toil and success is credible.
The principle applies to Torah study, where success depends on heaven for retention only; business success depends on heaven generally.
R. Yitzchak introduces advice about wicked people who prosper.
Advice: when you see a wicked man favored by fortune, do not contend with him.
Psalm verses cited to show the wicked prosper, are vindicated, and triumph over enemies.
Objection: R. Yohanan taught in R. Shimon b. Yohai's name that contending with the wicked is permitted.
Proverbs verse: those who keep the law contend with the wicked.
Baraita of R. Dostai b. Matun: contending with the wicked is permitted in this world.
Rebuttal: the whisperer who says do not contend is one whose conscience troubles him.
Reply: the verses mean not to become like the wicked, not that contending is forbidden.
Proverbs verse: let not your heart envy sinners.
No contradiction: one saying concerns personal matters, the other religious matters.
Alternatively, both concern personal matters, and still no contradiction arises.
The difference: one speaks of a wholly righteous person, the other of one not wholly righteous.
R. Huna cites Habakkuk: the wicked can swallow one more righteous than himself, but not a wholly righteous person.
Alternatively, when fortune smiles on the wicked, the case differs.
Ulla describes Rome as a great city with 365 markets and dimensions of 300 parasangs.
The king dines daily in one market; residents receive royal portions, and the city has baths, windows, and natural boundaries.
Mishnah: if the Megillah was read in the first Adar and the year was intercalated, it is read again in the second Adar; the only difference is the Megillah and gifts to the poor.
Gemara: this implies the special portions are the same in both Adars.
Asks which authority the Mishnah follows.
The Mishnah follows neither the First Tanna, R. Eliezer b. R. Yose, nor Rabban Shimon b. Gamaliel, as a baraita shows.
Baraita: all mitzvot done in Adar II may be done in Adar I, except the reading of the Megillah, which is read again in Adar II.
R. Eliezer b. R. Yose: the Megillah is not read again in Adar II, since all mitzvot of Adar II are done in Adar I.
R. Shimon b. Gamaliel in R. Yose's name: the Megillah is read again in Adar II, and both agree on mourning and fasting.
Asks whether R. Shimon b. Gamaliel here equals the First Tanna.
R. Papa: they differ on special portions, which the First Tanna would read in Adar II ab initio but not require again.
R. Eliezer b. R. Yose permits the Megillah ab initio in Adar I, while R. Shimon requires even special portions to be repeated in Adar II.
Asks which authority the Mishnah follows, given the difficulty each option faces.
The Mishnah follows the First Tanna; mention of the Megillah implies gifts too, since they depend on each other.
Alternatively, the Mishnah follows Rabban Shimon b. Gamaliel, with an omitted clause.
Reconstruction: the Mishnah's Adar rule covers only Megillah and gifts, with mourning and fasting the same, and special portions not addressed.
R. Hiyya b. Abin in R. Yohanan's name: the halakhah follows Rabban Shimon b. Gamaliel, who spoke in R. Yose's name.
R. Yohanan: both sides derive their views from the same verse, 'in every year'.
R. Eliezer b. R. Yose reasons that as Adar usually follows Shevat, so here Adar is next to Shevat.
R. Shimon b. Gamaliel reasons that as Adar usually follows Nisan, so here Adar is next to Nisan.
Asks why R. Shimon would delay Purim to Adar II, when R. Eliezer's reasoning seems more compelling.
R. Tabi: R. Shimon wants Purim's redemption near Pesah's, so the observances fall in adjacent months.
R. Elazar: R. Shimon's reason comes from the verse on the second letter of Purim.
Esther verse: 'to confirm this letter of Purim, the second' is cited.
Gemara: the verse was necessary to be written.

7a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara continues: it was necessary to write the word second.
Both 'every year' and 'second' are written, because each alone would suggest a different reading.
Asks what R. Eliezer b. R. Yose does with the word second.
He needs it for R. Shmuel b. Yehuda's teaching that Purim was first decreed in Shushan, then throughout the world.
Shmuel b. Yehuda's account: Esther asked the sages to establish Purim, and they cited the risk of nations' jealousy.
Variant teaching: Esther asked the sages to write her account for the ages, and they replied with Proverbs.
Proverbs verse: have I not written for you three times, with thirds and not fourths.
Until they found a verse in the Torah: Exodus instructs to write a memorial in a book.
Exposition of 'write this, memorial, book': what is written here, in Deuteronomy, the Prophets, and the Megillah.
Like the following tannaim, the exegesis is given in a different order.
R. Joshua and R. Elazar HaModai each give their own division of the three terms.
Shmuel holds that the Megillah of Esther does not defile the hands.
Objection: does Shmuel deny Esther was inspired, when he said elsewhere that it was?
Objection from a baraita: R. Meir, R. Yose and R. Shimon disagree about Koheleth and the Song of Songs.
R. Shimon b. Menasia: Koheleth does not defile the hands because it is Solomon's wisdom.
Objection: was that all Solomon composed?
Scripture verses cited: Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs, and one must not add to his words.
The second verse warns that Solomon did not write everything he said, only what was fitting.
R. Eliezer and R. Akiva each hold Esther was inspired, citing verses about Haman and Esther's favor.
R. Meir and R. Yose b. Durmaskit each hold Esther was inspired, citing verses about Mordecai and the spoil.
Shmuel: had he been there, he would have given a superior proof, since those above confirmed what the people accepted below.
Rava: all these proofs can be refuted except Shmuel's; R. Elazar's proof can be answered as Haman's self-interest.
R. Akiva's proof can be refuted by R. Elazar's reading that each man saw Esther as his own nation's.
R. Meir's proof can be refuted by R. Hiyya b. Abba's reading of Bigtan and Teresh as men from Tarshish.
R. Yose b. Durmaskit's proof can be refuted by the idea that messengers were sent; Shmuel's cannot be refuted.
Ravina's proverb: one grain of sharp pepper is better than a basket of pumpkins.
R. Joseph: the days of Purim shall not cease among the Jews, from Esther 9:28.
R. Nahman b. Yitzchak: their memorial shall not cease from their descendants, from Esther 9:28.
The Gemara introduces the mitzvah of gifts to the poor.
Baraita of R. Joseph: sending portions means two portions to one person, and gifts to the poor means two gifts to two people.
Judah Nesiah sent R. Oshaia a calf's leg and a barrel of wine.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mari's reply thanking Rabbah for fulfilling the mitzvah of portions and gifts.
Rabbah sends a gift to Mari through Abaye, who predicts Mari's reaction.
Mari returns a contrasting gift, which Abaye anticipates as a playful reversal.
Abaye describes the many dishes served at Mari's house and his delight in them.
Abaye offers two proverbs about hunger and the appetite for sweet things.
Abaye and Abaye's companion habitually swapped their meals with each other.
Rava teaches that one must drink on Purim until unable to tell Haman from Mordecai.
Rabbah and R. Zera's Purim feast ends in tragedy, revival, and a refusal to repeat it.
Rava rules that a Purim feast eaten at night fails the obligation, citing a verse.
Setting: R. Ashi sits before R. Kahana while the expected rabbis have not arrived.
Ashi asks why the rabbis are late, suggesting they may be busy feasting.
Kahana asks whether the rabbis could simply have feasted the night before.
Ashi asks whether the master has not heard Rava's ruling on night feasts.
The recited ruling: a Purim feast eaten at night does not discharge the obligation.
Kahana asks whether Rava actually said this.
Ashi confirms that Rava indeed said it.
Ashi repeated Rava's ruling forty times until he firmly memorized it.
Mishnah: festivals differ from Shabbat only regarding preparing food.
Gemara infers that preliminaries to food preparation are equal on both days.
The Mishnah cannot follow R. Judah, since a baraita states the opposing position.
The baraita quotes R. Judah permitting even preliminaries to food preparation on festivals.
What is the reasoning of the first Tanna against R. Judah's permission?
R. Judah reads the verse's 'for you' as covering all of your requirements.
The first Tanna objects that the same 'for you' wording appears in other verses.
Reply: the two verses apply to preliminaries doable the day before and those not.
Mishnah: Shabbat and Yom Kippur differ only in the court or karet penalty.
Gemara infers that the two days are equal regarding monetary compensation.
Whose view does this Mishnah follow?
It follows R. Nehunia b. HaKaneh, who treated Yom Kippur like Shabbat for compensation.
Elsewhere taught: one liable to karet who is flogged is exempt from karet.
Verse 'your brother' shows that a flogged offender is then like a brother.
R. Hananiah b. Gamaliel's position, as stated in that teaching.
R. Yohanan reports that R. Hananiah's colleagues disagreed with him.
Rava reports the school of Rav's version of the Mishnah's distinction.
If Hananiah's view is right, both days would be punished by human courts.
Rav Nahman identifies the view as R. Yitzchak's: karet offenders are not flogged.
Baraita: R. Yitzchak holds karet offenders are included in the general prohibition.
Why is karet specifically mentioned for relations with one's sister?
To show she is punished by karet and not by lashes.
R. Ashi reconciles all views: even the Rabbis hold the same essential distinction.

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: a vow against food and a vow against benefit differ only regarding standing on property and non-food vessels.
Gemara infers that vessels used for preparing food are treated alike under both vows.
Objection: people are not particular about standing on property, so the distinction seems pointless.
Rava names the source as R. Elazar, who forbids even what is normally tolerated under such a vow.
Mishnah: vowed and freewill offerings differ only in whether the owner must replace them.
Gemara infers that the two kinds of offering are equal regarding the prohibition of delay.
We learned elsewhere how to define a vow versus a freewill offering by the wording used.
What is the practical difference between a vow and a freewill offering?
Vowed animals must be replaced if they die or are stolen; freewill animals need not be.
From where is this rule derived?
Baraita: the verse's phrase 'upon him' is read by R. Shimon as limiting replacement liability.
What does the word 'upon' imply here?
R. Yitzchak bar Avdimi: saying 'upon myself' is like taking the animal on one's shoulder.
Mishnah: a zav who sees two discharges and one who sees three differ only in the sacrifice.
Gemara infers that the two cases are equal regarding bed, seat, and counting seven days.
From where is this rule derived?
Baraita of R. Simai: the text counts two issues for impurity and three for a sacrifice.
Explanation: two issues make him impure, and three also require a sacrifice.
Objection: perhaps two issues bring a sacrifice without impurity, and three cause impurity.
Rejection: this cannot be meant, as a baraita shows otherwise.
Baraita on 'from his issue' (Leviticus 15:15): some zavim bring sacrifices and some do not.
Baraita explains: three issues bring a sacrifice, while two issues do not.
Objection: perhaps one must have had three before bringing a sacrifice at two issues.
Both R. Simai and the verse 'from his issue' are needed to establish the rule fully.
If 'from his issue' is used for a derashah, what does the phrase derive from the cleansing verse?
Baraita: 'from his issue' teaches that a zav with two observations must count seven days.
Can this not be deduced logically: if he defiles bed and seat, he should need seven days?

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A counterexample: a woman who counts day by day defiles bed and seat yet need not count seven days.
Conclusion: the zav's logical argument may fail the same way, so it cannot establish the seven-day count.
The verse from his issue, he shall count, implies a zav with two observations must count seven days.
Rav Papa asks Abaye why one 'from his issue' includes and the other excludes a zav with two observations.
If the word were meant to exclude, the verse could omit it; logic alone could be countered by the day-by-day woman.
The word is needed to show cleansing of the issue alone, not of issue and leprosy; hence the zav counts seven days.
Mishnah: a metzora under observation differs from a definite metzora only in hair and garments, and clean ones only in shaving and birds.
Gemara infers that the two cases are equal regarding being sent out of the camp and defiling.
From where is this rule derived?
Baraita of R. Shmuel b. Yitzchak: the priest's pronouncement of cleanness reads as the metzora being clean from the outset.
Rava objects: then the zav's washing and cleansing would also need to mean being clean from the outset.
Rather, cleanness means being clean now as to not defiling vessels retroactively, and likewise for the metzora.
Rava derives from the verse about the metzora with plague in him that only a bodily plague requires sending out.
Abaye objects: then the verse about all the days of plague would exclude a day-based metzora from sending out.
Objection: the Mishnah's wording implies equal status for sending out and for defiling by entering.
Reply: the words all the days include the metzora under observation within the rule of sending out.
If so, why is such a metzora not required to shave and bring birds, as the Mishnah states?
Abaye: the verse about the priest going out and the plague being healed excludes day-based cases from sending out.
Mishnah: scrolls may be written in any language, while tefillin and mezuzot only in Assyrian script; Rabban Shimon b. Gamaliel adds Greek.
Gemara infers that for stitching with sinews and defiling the hands the two are the same.
Scrolls may be written in any language, as the Mishnah states.
Contradiction from a baraita: Hebrew text in Aramaic script, or Aramaic in Hebrew, does not defile the hands unless Assyrian.
Rava replies: there is no contradiction.

9a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The two statements differ: one concerns books in our script, the other books in their script.
Abaye objects: if the baraita means foreign script, why mention Aramaic in Hebrew, since Hebrew in Hebrew also needs Assyrian.
Reply: there is no contradiction, since one statement follows the Rabbis and the other R. Shimon b. Gamaliel.
Objection: if the view is R. Shimon b. Gamaliel's, then Greek should still be allowed, which he does not.
Reply: the statements concern scrolls on one side and tefillin and mezuzot on the other.
What is the reason tefillin and mezuzot must be written in Hebrew?
Because the verse says and they shall be, meaning they must remain as originally written.
Which Aramaic passages in the Torah could be written in Hebrew, and what case applies to tefillin?
Reply: the baraita refers to the Megillah on one side and other books on the other.
The Megillah is written according to their writing and their language, per Esther 1:20.
What Aramaic in the Megillah could be written in Hebrew?
R. Papa and R. Nahman cite Esther 1:20 words, pitgam and yekar, as examples of foreign words.
R. Ashi: the baraita refers to other books, following R. Judah's view that tefillin and mezuzot need Assyrian script.
Objection: the verse and they shall be implies the First Tanna forbade Greek, yet the Rabbis permitted it.
Reply: the Rabbis permitted Greek only in the sense of a scroll of the Torah.
Baraita: R. Judah says even when the Rabbis permitted Greek, it was only for a Torah scroll.
The reason: King Ptolemy gathered seventy-two elders who each translated the Torah identically under divine inspiration.
The translators changed verses such as Genesis 1:1 and 1:26 to avoid misreading.
They altered Genesis 2:2 and 5:2, for example writing rested rather than created them.
They altered Genesis 11:7 and 18:12 to avoid anthropomorphic or misleading phrasing.
They altered Genesis 49:6 to avoid a harsh description of Jacob's sons.
They altered Exodus 4:20 so Moses made his family ride on a carrier rather than men.
They altered Exodus 12:40 to clarify the four hundred years of dwelling in Egypt and other lands.
They altered Exodus 24:5 and 24:11 to avoid implying Israel's nobles were harmed or disrespected.

9b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Verses cited as examples of the Greek translators' changes to the wording of the Torah.
Ptolemy's wife was named hare, so the translators wrote a different animal to avoid mockery.
R. Shimon b. Gamaliel holds that even books of Scripture may be written only in Greek.
R. Abbahu, in R. Yohanan's name, rules that the halakhah follows R. Shimon b. Gamaliel.
What is the reason for R. Shimon b. Gamaliel's view?
Genesis 9:27 says God will enlarge Yefet and he will dwell in the tents of Shem, read as Yefet's words in Shem's tents.
Objection: why not read the verse as referring to Gomer and Magog?
R. Hiyya b. Abba: the verse says Yefet's beauty, not Gomer and Magog, shall dwell in Shem's tents.

Mishnah: an anointed priest and one wearing extra garments differ only regarding the bull for unwitting transgressions, and a serving High Priest and a former one differ only in the Yom Kippur bull and the tenth-ephah.
Gemara infers that the Yom Kippur bull and the tenth-ephah are treated equally for both kinds of priest.
The Mishnah does not follow R. Meir.
Baraita: R. Meir holds one wearing extra garments brings the bull, while the Sages disagree.
What is the reason for R. Meir's view?
Leviticus 4:3 says the anointed priest, and the word anointed teaches that wearing garments also qualifies.
The Mishnah is explained as not following R. Meir.
What about the end of the Mishnah, which can be read as making all other matters equal?
Baraita: when a replacement high priest was appointed and the first is restored, R. Meir says the second retains all high priesthood duties.
R. Yose: the first returns to service, while the second is not fit to serve as high priest or ordinary priest.
R. Yose recounts the case of R. Yosef b. Ulam, whose removal and replacement were judged by the Sages to follow the first.
Reasons: a high priest is not demoted to avoid enmity, and holiness is raised but never lowered.
Are we to say the first clause follows the Sages and the second follows R. Meir?
Hisda says yes; R. Joseph says the Mishnah reflects R. Judah the Prince combining differing tannaim.
Mishnah: great and small altars differ only in the Passover offering; anything that may be vowed or freewill-offered may be brought on the small altar.
Is the Passover offering alone meant, or things like it?
The view is attributed to R. Shimon, whose position is then cited.
Baraita of R. Shimon: even the congregation offered only Passover and fixed-time obligatory sacrifices on the altars.
Mishnah: Shiloh and Jerusalem differ only in where lesser holy offerings and second tithe could be eaten.
In both places the most holy offerings were eaten within the curtains; then Shiloh's sanctity is noted.

10a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Altars were permitted after Shiloh's sanctity but not after Jerusalem's sanctity.
R. Yitzchak reports that sacrifices may be offered in Onias's temple, since the first holiness was temporary.
Deuteronomy 12:9 compares rest, Shiloh, to inheritance, Jerusalem, so both were later permitted again.
They ask R. Yitzchak whether he really said this.
Rava confirms that R. Yitzchak did say it and that he learned it from him.
Why did R. Yitzchak retract his view?
Because R. Mari raised a difficulty: after Jerusalem's sanctity no permission was ever restored.
A tannaitic dispute: R. Eliezer's baraita on how the walls and curtains of the Temple were built.
R. Joshua's baraita: sacrifices, holy foods, and second tithe remain valid because Jerusalem was sanctified for all time.
Inference: R. Eliezer holds Jerusalem was not sanctified for all time.
Ravina objects to R. Ashi: perhaps all agree the first holiness was for all time, and they report different traditions.
The curtains were required by R. Eliezer only for privacy.
Rather, the view follows R. Ishmael b. R. Yose: the first holiness was for its time, not for the future.
Contradiction: R. Ishmael b. R. Yose's other teaching says the Sages listed the walled cities for a reason.
The Sages listed them because the returning exiles found those cities walled and sanctified them.

10b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara: the verse-based sanctity was not needed for these cities; they were simply found and listed, and the same applies to any walled city with a tradition.
Objection: the two statements attributed to R. Ishmael b. R. Yose seem to contradict each other.
Reply: either two Tannaim report R. Ishmael differently, or the latter is R. Eleazar b. Yose's teaching.
Baraita of R. Eleazar b. Yose: a walled city keeps its status even if it lacks a wall now, having had one before.
R. Levi, or R. Yonatan, relays a tradition from the Men of the Great Assembly: vayehi signals approaching trouble.
Esther 1:1: vayehi in the days of Ahashverosh, and Haman appears in the story.
Further vayehi examples: Ruth 1:1 with famine, and Genesis 6 with human wickedness.
More vayehi examples: Genesis 11 and 14 with the building of a city and a war.
Vayehi examples from Joshua: the angel with a drawn sword, and Israel's trespass.
Vayehi examples from Samuel: a man of Ramathaim and Hannah's barren womb.
Vayehi when Samuel was old, and his sons did not walk in his ways.
Vayehi with David's success and Saul's enmity toward him.
Vayehi with Saul's hostility, paired with the parallel vayehi examples.
Vayehi when the king dwelt in his house, followed by the prohibition on building the Temple.
Kings I 8:19: you shall not build the house, showing vayehi often signals trouble.
Objection: Leviticus 9:1 uses vayehi on the eighth day, which seems to be a happy occasion.
Baraita: that day brought joy before God like the day heaven and earth were created.
Comparison: the eighth day uses vayehi, and the creation day uses vayehi with one day.
Nadav and Avihu died on that eighth day, so the joy was mixed with trouble.
Objection: other vayehi passages, such as Kings I 6:1, Genesis 29:1, and Genesis 1:5, do not signal trouble.
R. Ashi: vayehi sometimes has this sense and sometimes not, but vayehi in the days of always signals trouble.
Five occurrences of vayehi in the days of, all in the verses cited, each connected with trouble.
R. Levi relays a tradition from our fathers: Amoz and Amaziah were brothers.
What does this tradition teach us?
R. Shmuel b. Nahmani in R. Yonatan's name: a modest bride in her father-in-law's house merits kings and prophets among her descendants.
How do we know this?
From Tamar: Judah thought her a harlot because she covered her face, and the verse shows he did not know her.
Her covering in her father-in-law's house meant she was not recognized, and she merited kings from David.
Prophets as well, as R. Levi held: Amoz and Amaziah were brothers, and Isaiah was son of Amoz.
R. Levi: a tradition that the ark took up no space within the Sanctuary.
Baraita: the ark of Moses had ten cubits of empty space on every side.
Kings I 6 verses on the Sanctuary and cherubim measurements show the room and wings' space.
Where then was the ark itself, if it occupied no space?
The ark stood miraculously without occupying any room.
R. Jonathan's exposition of Isaiah 54:22: name is script, remnant is language, offshoot is kingdom, and offspring is Vashti.
R. Shmuel b. Nahmani opens with Isaiah 55:13 on thorn and brier.
The thorn is wicked Haman, who set himself up as an idol; the cypress is Mordecai.
Mordecai is the chief of spices, as Exodus 30:23 says, flowing myrrh (mor).
The Aramaic rendering of that verse: mare deki.
The brier is wicked Vashti, daughter of Nebuchadnezzar, and the Song of Songs verse about gold.
The myrtle is virtuous Esther, called Hadassah, as Esther 2:7 says.
The Megillah reading is named a name and an everlasting sign, which refers to the days of Purim.
R. Joshua b. Levi opens with Deuteronomy 28:63 on God rejoicing over the wicked's downfall.
Objection: Chronicles II 20:21 says give thanks for his mercy endures, while R. Yohanan notes for he is good is omitted.
R. Yohanan's reading of Exodus 14:20: the angels wished to sing while the Egyptians drowned.
God rebukes the angels: my creatures are drowning in the sea, and you sing praise.
R. Elazar: God does not rejoice himself, but makes others rejoice, as the text yasis shows.
R. Abba b. Kahana opens with Ecclesiastes 2:26 on wisdom, knowledge and joy.
Ecclesiastes 2:26 read as: the good man is Mordecai; the sinner is Haman; Esther set Mordecai over Haman's house.
R. Rabbah b. Ofran opens with Jeremiah 49:38 on the king and princes.
The king is Vashti, and the princes are Haman and his ten sons.
R. Dimi b. Isaac opens a further exposition from the same verse.

11a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ezra 9:9 says Israel was not forsaken in bondage but found mercy before the kings of Persia.
When did this happen?
R. Hanina b. Papa's verse Psalms 66:12: fire under Nebuchadnezzar, water under Pharaoh, abundance under Haman.
R. Yohanan's verse Psalms 98:3 is applied to the days of Mordecai and Esther.
Resh Lakish's verse Proverbs 28:15: the roaring lion is Nebuchadnezzar, as Jeremiah 4:7 shows.
The ravenous bear is Ahashverosh, as Daniel 7:5 describes the bear.
R. Joseph taught that the bear-like Persians eat, grow fat, and have no rest like bears.
The wicked ruler is Haman, and the poor people are Israel, poor in mitzvot.
R. Elazar opens with Ecclesiastes 10:18 on laziness and the house leaking.
Israel's laziness in not occupying itself with Torah made the Holy One's enemy prosper.
Leviticus 27:8 gives the meaning of makh as poor, and Psalms 104:3 shows the Holy One lays the beams.
R. Nahman b. Isaac's Psalms 124 reading: if not for the Lord, a man rose against us, not a king.
Rava's Proverbs 29:2: the righteous Mordecai and Esther bring joy, while Haman brings sighing.
Matanah and R. Ashi each cite Deuteronomy 4 on God being near to Israel.
Rav reads vayehi as voi, trouble, citing Deuteronomy 28:68 on selling into slavery.
Shmuel reads Leviticus 26:44 as marking successive eras: Greeks, Nebuchadnezzar, Haman, Persians, Gog and Magog.
A baraita expands Leviticus 26:44 with named heroes in each era: Daniel, the Hasmoneans, Mordecai and Esther, and the Sages.
R. Levi cites Numbers 33:55 on not driving out the inhabitants of the land.
R. Hiyya cites Numbers 33:56: as I intended to do to them, so I will do to you.
Rav: Ahashverosh is the brother and counterpart of the head, meaning Nebuchadnezzar.
Daniel 2:38 calls Nebuchadnezzar the head of gold; Ezra 4:6 reports the accusation against Judah under Ahashverosh.
Shmuel: Israel's faces were blackened in his days like the sides of a pot.
R. Yohanan: everyone who thought of him cried alas for my head.
R. Hanina: all became poor in his days, as Esther 10:1 says he laid a tribute.
The hu-construction shows the wicked persisted in wickedness from start to end, as with Ahashverosh, Esau, Dathan, and Ahaz.
Parallel examples of persistence in righteousness: Abraham, Aaron and Moses, and David's humility before greater men.
Rav: 'who reigned' means Ahashverosh made himself king; opinions differ on whether this was to his credit.
Rav and Shmuel dispute whether Hodu and Cush are at opposite ends of the world or next to each other.
Similarly I Kings 5:4 describes Solomon's dominion from Tiphsah to Gaza.
Rav and Shmuel dispute whether Tiphsah and Gaza mark the ends of the world.
R. Hisda: he first ruled over seven, then twenty, and finally a hundred provinces.
Objection: the Amram verse Exodus 6:20 counts years, but the counting here is an extra verse.
What is the derivation, since the verse is extra and the count is written as 127 provinces?
A baraita: three kings ruled by trickery: Ahab, Ahashverosh, and Nebuchadnezzar.
Ahab's oath in I Kings 18:10 shows he was made to swear by a nation he did not rule.
If he ruled over them, how could he make them swear?
Nebuchadnezzar ruled over the nations by Jeremiah 27:8, which shows the king of Babylon as ruler.
This is what we said about Ahashverosh: the same trickery applied to him.

11b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection that Solomon also failed to keep his kingdom, so the list of exceptions seems incomplete.
Reply that the problem works out on the view that a king is first king and then commoner.
Asks what can be said on the view that the sequence is king, commoner, and king again.
Solomon's case is different: he ruled over both the upper and the lower worlds.
Scriptural support from Chronicles that Solomon sat on the throne of God.
Objection that Sennacherib seems to be a counterexample to the claim.
Quotes Sennacherib's boast from Isaiah as support for the objection.
Reply that Sennacherib never conquered Jerusalem, so it is an exception.
Objection that Darius seems to be a counterexample as well.
Quotes Darius's decree to all peoples from Daniel as support.
Reply that there were seven provinces Darius never ruled.
Quotes Daniel's account of the 120 satraps Darius appointed.
Objection that Cyrus also seems to rule the whole world.
Quotes Cyrus's decree that God gave him all the kingdoms of the earth.
Reply that Cyrus was merely boasting about himself.
Raises a contradiction between two verses about when Ahasuerus reigned.
Asks what the phrase when he sat actually means.
Explains it as after his mind had settled and he felt secure.
Asserts that the king reasoned he would calculate correctly where Belshazzar erred.
Asks what this reasoning refers to.
Cites Jeremiah and Daniel on seventy years of desolation of Jerusalem.
Explains how the seventy years are reckoned and that the Temple vessels were used.
Asks how we know that Nebuchadnezzar reigned forty-five years.
Cites a baraita listing the exile years of the kings.
Explains the baraita by matching exile years to the reigns of the kings.
Quotes Jeremiah 52:31 on the release of Jehoiachin.
Adds the years together to reach the total of seventy.
Belshazzar's assertion that they will not be redeemed, so he used the Temple vessels.
Cites Daniel's words to Belshazzar and the verse on his death that night.
Cites Daniel 6:1 on Darius receiving the kingdom at about sixty-two years old.
Ahasuerus's reasoning that he would calculate correctly and not err.
Asks whether the verse says kingdom of Babylon or to Babylon.
Explains to Babylon as referring to the exile of Babylon.
Asks how many years are to be subtracted, and gives eight as the number.
Explains that one year of Belshazzar and Darius and Cyrus are inserted to make seventy.
Concludes that the reckoning now comes to seventy years.
Narrates that seeing seventy completed without redemption, he used the vessels, and Satan danced and Vashti was slain.
Objection that he reckoned correctly, so he should not be faulted.
Reply that he also erred, since he should have counted from the destruction of Jerusalem.
Asks how many years are short, and how long he reigned.
Concludes that in the fourteenth year he should have rebuilt the Temple.
Asks why Ezra's verse says the work of the house of God ceased.
Quotes Ezra 4:24 about the work on the house of God ceasing.
Rava explains that the years were not complete years.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita teaches that Darius completed one further year left to Babylon.
Rava asserts that Daniel also erred in this calculation.
Cites Daniel 9:2 and infers from the word meditated that Daniel had erred.
Points out that the two verses about Babylon and Jerusalem contradict each other.
Quotes the two conflicting verses from Jeremiah and Daniel.
Rava answers that the first verse only referred to charging, which was fulfilled.
Quotes Cyrus's decree in Ezra 1:2 to show the charge was fulfilled.
Introduces R. Nahman bar R. Hisda's exposition of a verse about Cyrus.
Asks what is meant by the verse about the Lord's anointed.
Quotes Isaiah 45:1 on the Lord's anointed, Cyrus.
Asks whether Cyrus was really the Messiah.
God complains to the Messiah that Cyrus was to build the Temple but did not.
Quotes Ezra 1:3 and Esther 1:3 on who went up and the army of Persia and Media.
Objects that elsewhere the verse lists the kings of Media before Persia.
Rava explains the Medes and Persians made a stipulation to supply kings and governors in turn.
Cites Esther 1:4 on the riches of his glorious kingdom.
R. Yose b. Hanina teaches that Ahasuerus dressed in priestly garments.
Compares the wording of Esther 1:4 with Exodus 28:2 to support R. Yose.
Rav and Shmuel dispute whether Ahasuerus was clever or foolish, with their reasons.
Disciples ask R. Shimon b. Yohai why Israel's enemies in that generation were destroyed.
R. Shimon tells them to give the answer themselves.
They reply that the enemies enjoyed the wicked king's feast.
Objects that the decree should then have covered all the world, not only Shushan.
The disciples ask R. Shimon to explain instead.
R. Shimon explains that they bowed down to an idol.
Asks whether God showed favoritism in the matter.
God only pretended to destroy them, just as they only pretended to worship.
Cites Lamentations 3:33 and Esther 1:5 about the court of the garden of the palace.
Rav's view on which guests were placed in court, garden, and palace.
Shmuel's view that they were placed in the court first and then moved inside.
A baraita teaches that the king seated them in the court and opened two doors.
Quotes Esther 1:6 on white, fine cotton, and blue.
Asks what hur means in the verse.
Rav says hur is lace-work, and Shmuel says white silk carpets.
R. Yose b. Hanina explains karpas as velvet cushions, and the couches and rods as silver and gold.
R. Judah teaches that couches matched the guests' worth, silver or gold.
R. Nehemiah objects that this would cause jealousy at the banquet.
Reply that the couches were silver and their feet gold.
R. Assi explains the stones as ones that cause their owners hard labor.
Cites Zechariah 9:16 as support for R. Assi's explanation.
Rav explains dar and sohareth as rows upon rows of marble.
Shmuel explains the dar as a precious stone that lit the banquet like midday.
A teaching of the school of R. Ishmael reads deror as tax remission for merchants.
Quotes Esther 1:7 on the vessels, and asks why the phrase diverse is needed.
Rava reports a heavenly voice warning that the earlier generation perished over vessels.
Rav teaches that each guest was given wine older than himself.
Quotes Esther 1:8 on the drinking being according to law.
Asks what is meant by according to law.
R. Hanan in R. Meir's name explains that the feast had more food than drink, as in Torah law.
Quotes the phrase none did compel from the verse.
R. Elazar teaches that each guest was given wine from his own country.
Rava reads the phrase according to every man's pleasure as referring to Mordecai and Haman.
Cites the verses calling Mordecai a Jewish man and Haman an adversary.
Quotes Esther 1:9 on Vashti's feast for the women in the royal house.
Rava explains both Ahasuerus and Vashti intended to transgress, and offers a proverb.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites the verse about the king's heart being merry with wine on the seventh day.
Asks whether the king's heart was not already merry with wine until then.
Rava explains that Shabbat feasts of Israel open with Torah and praise, unlike idolaters' frivolity.
At that wicked feast, guests argued over whether Median or Persian women were most beautiful.
Ahasuerus says his vessel is Chaldean, not Median or Persian, and offers to show her.
The guests agree, on condition that she appear naked.
Measure for measure: Vashti used to strip Israelite women and make them work on Shabbat.
Quotes Esther 2:1 that the king remembered Vashti and what was decreed against her.
Recalls that Vashti was immodest and that both intended transgression.
Asks why she would not come when summoned.
R. Yose b. Hanina says leprosy broke out on her, and a baraita adds Gabriel gave her a tail.
Quotes the verse saying the king was very angry.
Asks why his anger burned so much.
Rava explains her reply insulted him as a stable master's son, which made him rage.
Quotes the verse where the king spoke to the wise men.
Identifies the wise men as the rabbis who knew how to fix calendar years and months.
The king tells them to judge Vashti for him.
The sages ask among themselves what they should do.
They weigh the dilemma: executing her now, or releasing her, given that she disrespected royalty.
They tell the king they cannot judge capital cases since the Temple's destruction.
Advice to go to Ammon and Moab, who remained settled like wine on its lees.
The sages explain their advice was well-founded, as the verse states.
Quotes Jeremiah 48:11 on Moab and then the names of the officers in Esther 1:14.
R. Levi says the whole verse concerns sacrifices.
Ministering angels ask God, name by name, whether the nations ever offered sacrifices as Israel did.
Cites Exodus 28:20 on the stones of the priestly garments.
Angels ask whether Israel ever performed the blood, grain and table offerings before God.
Quotes the verse with the name Memucan.
A Tanna teaches Memucan is Haman, named for being destined for punishment.
Rav Kahana says the common man pushes himself forward to rule his own house.
Rava says that without the first letters none of Israel's enemies would remain.
People ask what the king meant by sending word that every man should rule his house.
People reply that it is obvious, since even a weaver must be in charge at home.
Quotes the verse where the king appointed officers.
Rav asks what verse this refers to.
Quotes Proverbs 13:16 on the clever man and the fool.
The clever man refers to David.
Quotes 1 Kings 1:2 where David's servants sought a young virgin for the king.
The fool refers to Ahasuerus, who ordered the daughters brought in.
Quotes Esther 2:3 and 2:5 about the officers and the Jew named Mordecai.
Asks why, if this is a pedigree, it does not trace back to Benjamin, and why these names are listed.
A Tanna explains the names Yair, Shimei and Kish as descriptive epithets, and notes Mordecai is called both Judean and Benjamite.
R. Nahman says Mordecai was crowned with good names and was distinguished by his customs.
Rabbah b. Bar Hanah reports that R. Joshua b. Levi said his father was from Benjamin and mother from Judah.
The rabbis say the tribes competed over Mordecai, each claiming him.
Rava says the community of Israel reverses the designations: a Judean wronged me, and a Benjamite repaid me.

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The tribes' claims continue: David spared Shimei and Saul spared Agag, the ancestors of Mordecai and Haman.
R. Yohanan says Mordecai indeed came from Benjamin.
Asks why Mordecai is nonetheless called a Jew.
Because he denied idolatry, and anyone who denies idolatry is called a Jew.
Cites Daniel 3:12 where certain Jews are named as refusing idolatry.
R. Shimon b. Pazzi says all of Chronicles is one, and its inner meanings can be found.
Cites 1 Chronicles 4:18 about the sons of Bitya, daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered took.
Asks why she is called a Jewess.
She repudiated idolatry, so she is called a Jewess.
Cites Exodus 2:5 on Pharaoh's daughter going down to bathe in the river.
R. Yohanan says she went down to cleanse herself from her father's idols, and so she bore.
Asks: but she only brought Moses up, so how is it bore?
Anyone who raises an orphan in his house is credited by Scripture as if he bore him.
Yered is Moses.
Asks why he was called Yered.
Each name of Moses is explained by his deeds, such as manna descending and fencing breaches.
Father, father, father: he was a father in Torah, wisdom and prophecy.
Repeats the verse listing the sons of Bitya whom Mered took.
Asks whether Mered was really his name, since Caleb was his name.
God said that Caleb, who rebelled against the spies, would take the daughter who rebelled against idols.
Cites Esther 2:6 on those carried away from Jerusalem.
Rava says Mordecai went into exile of his own accord.
Cites Esther 2:7 on Mordecai bringing up Hadassah, who is also called Esther.
R. Meir says Esther was her proper name.
Asks why she was then called Hadassah.
Hadassah is after the righteous who are called myrtles.
Cites Zechariah 1:8 about the myrtle trees.
R. Yehuda says Hadassah was her name.
Asks why then she was called Esther.
Because she concealed the facts about herself.
Cites Esther 2:20 that Esther did not reveal her people or kindred.
R. Nehemiah says Hadassah was her name.
Asks why then she was called Esther.
All the nations called her that after Istahar.
Ben Azzai says Esther was neither tall nor short but of medium size like a myrtle.
R. Joshua b. Korha says Esther was green and had a thread of kindness drawn on her.
Cites Esther 2:7 that she had neither father nor mother.
Asks why the verse needed to say this again.
Aha explains her father died while she was conceived and her mother died at her birth.
Cites Esther 2:7 that Mordecai took her for a daughter.
A Tanna teaches in R. Meir's name to read for a house, meaning wife, not for a daughter.
Cites 2 Samuel 12:3 about the ewe lamb that was unto him as a daughter.
Asks whether it was like a daughter just because it lay in his bosom.
Rather it means like a wife, so here too it means a wife.
Cites Esther 2:9 on the seven maidens given to her.
Rava explains they were seven so she could count the days of the week by them.
Rav says he gave her Jewish food to eat.
Shmuel says he gave her pieces of pork.
R. Yohanan says he gave her legumes.
Cites Daniel 1:16 about the steward giving legumes, and Esther 2:12 on six months with oil of myrrh.
Asks what the oil of myrrh is.
R. Hiyya b. Abba says it is stakat.
R. Huna says it is olive oil not a third ripe.
A baraita teaches that R. Judah says anpikon is olive oil not a third ripe.
It is used for smearing because it removes hair and softens the skin.
R. Yohanan says from his disgrace we learn his credit: he did not have relations by day.
Cites Esther 2:15 that Esther found favor in everyone's eyes.
R. Elazar says she looked like a member of his own people to everyone.
Cites Esther 2:16 that she was taken to the king in the tenth month, Tevet.
Tevet is the month when one body benefits from being close to another.
Cites Esther 2:17 that the king loved Esther above all the virgins.
Rav says he sought to taste a virgin's flavor and found it, or a non-virgin's flavor and found it.
Cites Esther 2:18 that the king made a great feast.
Esther's feast, tax remissions, and gifts, yet she did not reveal who she was.
Cites Esther 2:19 on the virgins gathered a second time.
Mordecai's counsel that a woman is jealous of other women, yet she still did not reveal herself.
Cites Esther 2:10 that Esther did not make known her people or birthplace.
R. Elazar asks what is meant by the verse.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites Job 36:7 that God does not withdraw eyes from the righteous, read as reward for modesty.
Rachel's modesty earned Saul as a descendant, and Saul's modesty earned Esther.
Asks what modesty Rachel displayed.
Cites Genesis 29:12 where Jacob told Rachel he was her father's brother.
Asks whether he was really her father's brother, or only her cousin.
Jacob proposed marriage; Rachel said her father was a trickster Jacob could not outwit.
Jacob replied that he was a brother in trickery.
Asks whether it is permitted for the righteous to use trickery.
Jacob replies yes.
Cites 2 Samuel 22:27 about dealing purely with the pure and wily with the perverse.
Jacob asks what the trickery is.
Rachel explains her older sister and the signs she gave her.
At night Rachel says she will let her sister be ashamed, and hands over the tokens to Leah.
Cites Genesis 29:25 that in the morning it was Leah.
Asks whether up to then it had not been Leah.
It was only through the tokens Rachel gave that Jacob did not know until then, so Rachel was rewarded with Saul.
Asks what modesty Saul displayed.
Cites 1 Samuel 10:16 that Saul did not tell his uncle about the kingdom.
Saul merited that Esther descend from him.
R. Elazar says when God grants greatness to a man it passes to his descendants for all generations.
Cites Job 36:7 that God sets kings forever on the throne.
If a man becomes arrogant, God humbles him, and his descendants are humbled too.
Cites Job 36:8 about those bound in fetters.
Cites Esther 2:20 that Esther did Mordecai's commandment.
R. Jeremiah says she showed her menstrual blood to the Sages to rule on it.
Cites Esther 2:20 as when she was brought up with him.
Rabbah b. Lema, in Rav's name, says she rose from Ahasuerus's lap and sat in Mordecai's.
Cites Esther 2:21 that Mordecai sat in the king's gate and Bigtan and Teresh were enraged.
R. Hiyya b. Abba reports R. Yohanan's teaching that God angered masters for a righteous man.
God caused the master to be angry with his servants for the sake of Joseph, a righteous man.
Cites Genesis 41:12 about the young Hebrew servant with us.
Servants were moved against their master to perform a miracle for Mordecai.
Cites Esther 2:22 that the matter was known to Mordecai.
R. Yohanan says Bigtan and Teresh were Tarseans who plotted poison, unaware Mordecai knew seventy languages.
The two conspirators exchange words about their guard posts, each keeping his own.
Cites Esther 2:23 that the matter was investigated and found, so they were not at their posts.
Asks after what the verse about these things refers to.
Rava says after God created a healing for the blow.
Resh Lakish says God heals Israel before striking, unlike the other nations.
Cites Hosea 7:1 about healing Israel and uncovering the iniquity of Ephraim.
The other nations are struck first and only then healed.
Cites Isaiah 19:22 where the Lord smites Egypt and then heals.
Cites Esther 3:6 that it seemed contemptible to lay hands on Mordecai alone.
Rava explains first Mordecai alone, then his people, then the Rabbis.
The Rabbis say finally all the Jews, and the lot was cast.
A Tanna teaches that when the lot fell on Adar, Haman rejoiced greatly.
Haman thought Moses died in that month, unaware Moses died and was born on the seventh of Adar.
Cites Esther 3:8 that there is one people.
Rava says no one was as skilled at evil talk as Haman, who urged the king to destroy them.
The king asks whether there are rabbis among them, and Haman answers they are one people.
Responses to Haman's objections: they are scattered and do not bear fruit, and they live in all provinces.
Explains that their laws differ, they do not eat or marry with others, and they despise the throne.
Cites Esther 3:9 on Haman's offer of ten thousand talents of silver.
Resh Lakish says God foresaw Haman would weigh shekels against Israel, so Israel's shekels were anticipated.
The Mishnah teaches that on the first of Adar the proclamation about the shekalim is made.
Cites Esther 3:11 about the silver given to Haman and the people.
R. Abba says a concluding remark on the verse.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A parable: Ahasuerus and Haman are like two neighbors, one with a mound and one with a ditch, who swap their land.
Cites Esther 3:10 that the king removed his ring.
R. Abba b. Kahana says removing the ring did more good than forty-eight prophets and seven prophetesses.
A baraita teaches the prophets added nothing to the Torah except the reading of the Megillah.
Asks how the Sages derive the Megillah reading from the Torah.
R. Hiyya b. Abin: if deliverance from slavery merits song, deliverance from death merits it even more.
Asks why then Hallel is not said for miracles outside the Land of Israel, as with the Exodus.
A baraita teaches that lands were proper for song only before Israel entered the land.
R. Nahman says reading the Megillah is equivalent to Hallel.
Rava objects that Hallel praises servants of the Lord, not of Ahasuerus, so the analogy fails.
Objects that a baraita contradicts this, since after exile the lands again became proper.
Asks whether there were no more prophets, citing the verse about Ramataim-Tzophim.
Quotes 1 Samuel 1:1 about a man from Ramataim-Tzophim who was one of two hundred prophets.
Many prophets arose, but only prophecies with a lesson for future generations were written down.
R. Shmuel b. Nahmani: the name means a man from two heights facing one another.
R. Hanin: the name means a man from the most exalted rank.
Asks who the men of that rank were.
They were the sons of Korah.
Cites Numbers 26:11 that the sons of Korah did not die.
A Tanna taught they were assigned a special place in Gehinnom and stood there.
Asks who the seven prophetesses were.
Sarah, Miriam, Deborah, Hannah, Abigail, Hulda and Esther.
Cites Genesis 11:29 on Milkah and Yiskah.
R. Yitzhak says Yiskah is Sarah.
Asks why she was called Yiskah.
Because she saw visions by means of the holy spirit.
Cites Genesis 21:12 about listening to Sarah's voice.
Another explanation: Yiskah because everyone gazed at her beauty.
Cites Exodus 15:20 that Miriam the prophetess was the sister of Aaron.
Asks why she is called Aaron's sister and not Moses's sister.
R. Nahman in Rav's name: she prophesied while Aaron's sister that her mother would bear a saviour, and the house filled with light.
Her father kissed her head and said her prophecy had been fulfilled.
When the child was cast into the river, her father tapped her head and asked where her prophecy was.
Cites Exodus 2:4 and Judges 4:4 on Deborah the prophetess, a woman of flames.
Asks what is meant by a woman of flames.
Because she made wicks for the Temple.
Cites Judges 4:5 that she sat under the palm tree.
Asks why she sat under a palm tree.
R. Shimon b. Avshalom: to avoid seclusion, and the palm has one heart like Israel's single heart to their Father.
Cites 1 Samuel 2:1 on Hannah's prayer that her horn is exalted.
David and Solomon were anointed with a horn and their kingship lasted, while Saul and Yehu were anointed with a cruse.
Cites 1 Samuel 2:2 that there is none holy as the Lord.
R. Yehuda b. Menashya reads lebalotekha, meaning God outlasts His works, unlike flesh and blood.
Cites 1 Samuel 2:2 that there is no rock like our God.
No artist can give breath and spirit to a drawn figure, but God fashions a form within a form.
Cites 2 Samuel 25:20 that Abigail came down by the hidden side of the mountain.
Asks why it does not say from the mountain.
Rabbah b. Shmuel: she came about blood from the hidden parts, which she brought and showed him.
He said to her.
He asks whether blood is to be shown at night.
She replies: are capital cases tried at night?
He said to her again.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abigail argues that Naval is a rebel against the king and needs no trial.
She replies that Saul still lives and Naval's fame has not spread, so his name is not yet gone.
Cites 1 Samuel 25:33, where David blesses Abigail for keeping him from bloodshed.
Explains the word bloods as meaning she bared her thigh and he walked three parasangs by its light.
He asks her to lie with him, and she responds.
Cites 1 Samuel 25:31 that this shall be no stumbling-block to you.
Asks what the other thing is that this word implies.
It is the incident of Bathsheba, and so it eventually happened.
Cites 1 Samuel 25:29 and 25:31 on the soul of your lord bound in life and remember your handmaid.
R. Nahman cites proverbs: a woman who talks while she spins, and the goose that stoops while its eyes peer afar.
Cites 2 Kings 22:14 that Hilkiah and others went to Hulda the prophetess.
Asks how Hulda could prophesy when Jeremiah was there.
Hulda was a close relative of Jeremiah, and he did not object to her prophesying.
Asks why Josiah himself did not go to Jeremiah but sent to Hulda.
Because women are more merciful.
R. Yohanan says Jeremiah was absent, having gone to bring back the ten tribes.
Asks from where we know that the ten tribes returned.
Cites Ezekiel 7:13 that the seller shall not return to what is sold.
Asks whether a prophet would prophesy that the Jubilee would be abolished.
It teaches that Jeremiah brought the tribes back.
Cites 2 Kings 23:17 on Josiah ruling over them and the grave of the man of God.
Asks what connection Josiah had with the altar at Bethel.
It shows that Josiah reigned over them.
R. Nahman says we learn it from Hosea 6:11 that a harvest is appointed for Judah.
Cites Esther 5:1 that Esther clothed herself in royalty.
Asks why the verse does not say royal clothing.
It shows she clothed herself in the Holy Spirit, as the verb is used of spirit in Chronicles.
Cites 1 Chronicles 12:19 where the spirit clothed Amasai.
R. Nahman says it is not proper for women to be arrogant, and names two arrogant women.
Cites Judges 4:6 where Deborah sent for Barak.
Contrasts that Deborah did not go to him, while Huldah was sent to by the people.
Cites 2 Kings 22:15 that they spoke to the man and to the king.
R. Nahman says Hulda was a descendant of the sons of Joshua.
Cites 2 Kings 22:14 and Judges 2:9 on Timnath-heres and the son of Hasrah.
Rav Ina the elder objects to Rav Nahman that eight prophets were priests who came from the harlot Rahab.
Lists the eight prophets: Neriah, Baruch, Seraiah, Mahseiah, Jeremiah, Hilkiah, Hanamel and Shallum.
R. Yehuda adds that Hulda the prophetess was also descended from Rahab the harlot.
Cites 2 Kings 22:14 on Tikvah son of Harhas and Joshua 2:18 on the cord of scarlet thread.
Rav Ina the elder replies that she converted and married Joshua.
Asks whether Joshua had children, since 1 Chronicles 7:27 seems to give none.

15a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how we know that the fathers of those eight prophets were also prophets.
Ulla's rule: naming a father signals a prophet son of a prophet, and naming a town signals origin there.
A baraita: when a praiseworthy or reprehensible deed is mentioned, the man is son of a righteous or wicked man.
R. Nahman says Malachi is the same as Mordecai.
Asks why Mordecai was called Malachi.
Objects that Malachi, Mordecai and others all prophesied in the second year of Darius.
A baraita: R. Yehoshua b. Korha says Malachi is Ezra, and the Sages say it is his name.
R. Nahman says the view that Malachi is Ezra is reasonable.
Cites Malachi 2:11 on Judah profaning the holiness of the Lord by marrying a foreign god's daughter.
Asks who put away the foreign women, and answers Ezra.
Cites Ezra 10:2 about the foreign wives.
The Rabbis teach four beautiful women: Sarah, Rahab, Abigail and Esther, with the Vashti variant.
A baraita on how each woman's name, voice, memory and appearance inspired desire.
R. Isaac says whoever says Rahab Rahab will have a seminal emission.
R. Nahman objects that he says Rahab Rahab and nothing happens to him.
R. Isaac replies he meant one who knows her and was intimate with her.
Cites Esther 4:1 that Mordecai knew all that was done.
Asks what Mordecai cried out.
Rav says Haman raised himself above Ahasuerus; Shmuel says the upper king prevailed over the lower king.
Cites Esther 5:1 on the queen being exceedingly afraid.
Asks what the word vatithalhal means.
Rav says it means she became a niddah; R. Jeremiah says she needed to relieve herself.
Cites Esther 4:5 that Esther called Hatach.
Rav says Hatach is Daniel.
Asks why he was called Hatach.
Because he was cut down from his elevated position.
Shmuel says Hatach was because all affairs of state were decided by his voice.
Cites Esther 4:5 that she sent to know what this was and why this was.
R. Isaac says she suspected Israel transgressed the five books of the Torah, written on both sides.
Mordecai did not go to her, showing a recalcitrant answer need not be taken back.
Cites Esther 4:16 telling Mordecai to gather the Jews, which is not according to custom.
R. Abba says it was not according to custom, because it was now willing rather than forced.
Cites Esther 4:17 that Mordecai passed over.
Rav says he made the first day of Passover a fast, and Shmuel says he crossed a stream.
Cites Esther 5:1 that Esther put on royalty.
Asks why the verse does not say royal clothing.
R. Elazar in R. Hanina's name: the holy spirit clothed her.
Cites 1 Chronicles 12:19 where a spirit clothed Amasai.
R. Elazar in R. Hanina's name: do not hold lightly the blessing of an ordinary man.
The two great men blessed were David and Daniel.
Cites 2 Samuel 24:23 on Aravnah blessing David and Daniel 6:17 on Darius blessing Daniel.
R. Elazar in R. Hanina's name: do not hold lightly the curse of an ordinary man.
Cites Genesis 20:16 where Abimelech cursed Sarah with a covering of the eyes.
The curse was fulfilled in her seed.
Cites Genesis 27:1 that Isaac's eyes were dim in old age.
R. Elazar in R. Hanina's name: God puts in the water first, unlike flesh and blood, citing Jeremiah 10:13.
Whoever reports a saying in the name of the one who said it brings deliverance to the world, as Esther did.
A righteous man dies only for his own generation, like a pearl lost only to its owner.
Cites Esther 5:13 saying all this is worth nothing to me.
Asks whether seeing Mordecai in the gate justified Haman saying all this is worth nothing.
Haman says all this is worth nothing to him.
R. Hisda offers an analogy of two litigants coming to court, explaining Haman's reaction to Mordecai.

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Papa says Haman was also called the slave sold for bread, a name for his poverty.
Cites Esther 5:13 that all this is worth nothing to me.
Explains the verse teaches that all of that wicked man's treasures were engraved on his heart.
When Haman saw Mordecai sitting at the king's gate, he said all this is worth nothing to me.
R. Elazar in R. Hanina's name: God will be a crown on the head of every righteous man.
Cites Isaiah 28:5 on the Lord of Hosts being a crown of glory.
Asks what the crown of glory and diadem of beauty mean.
They are for those who do his will and await his glory.
Asks whether this is for all, since the verse says the residue of his people.
It is for whoever makes himself a mere remnant.
Explains the words of Isaiah 28:6 as referring to judging one's inclination, true judgment, subduing the passions, and disciples of the Sages.
The Attribute of Justice asks God why these differ from the others.
God replies that Israel toils in Torah and the nations do not; the others stumble and are sent to Gehinnom.
Cites 1 Samuel 25:31 where pukah means stumbling, as in Gehinnom.
Peliliyah refers to judges who give verdicts.
Cites Exodus 21:22 that he shall pay as the judges determine.
Cites Esther 5:1 that she stood in the inner court of the king's house.
R. Levi says the Divine Presence left her when she reached the chamber of idols.
Cites Psalms 22:2 as her cry, My God, why have you forsaken me.
Asks whether God judges the inadvertent sin like the intentional, or because she called him a dog.
Cites Psalms 22:21 that she called him a dog.
She retracted and called him a lion.
Cites Psalms 22:22 and Esther 5:2 on the king seeing Esther the queen.
R. Yohanan says three ministering angels helped her, one raising her head, one giving charm, one stretching the sceptre.
R. Jeremiah says the sceptre was two cubits and was made twelve cubits long.
Other variants give sixteen, twenty-four, and in a baraita sixty cubits.
The Gemara notes a similar stretching of Pharaoh's daughter's arm and of the teeth of the wicked.
Cites Psalms 3:8 where God broke the teeth of the wicked.
Resh Lakish reads it as shirbavta, and Rabbah b. Ofran cites R. Elazar that the sceptre was two hundred cubits.
Cites Esther 5:6 that the king offers her up to half the kingdom.
Asks what could divide the kingdom.
The building of the Temple.
Cites Esther 5:4 that the king and Haman come to the banquet.
Asks what Esther saw that led her to invite Haman.
R. Elazar says she set a trap for him.
Cites Psalms 69:23 on their table becoming a snare.
R. Joshua says she learned it from her father's house.
Cites Proverbs 25:21 that if your enemy is hungry, give him bread.
R. Meir says so that he should not take counsel and rebel.
R. Judah says so that they should not recognize that she is a Jew.
R. Nehemiah says so that Israel would not neglect prayer for mercy.
R. Yose says so that he would always be at hand for her, and R. Shimon b. Menassiah says to perhaps trigger a miracle.
R. Joshua b. Korha says she would encourage him to be killed, and Rabban Gamaliel says the king was fickle.
R. Gamaliel says we still need R. Eliezer of Modiin, who taught that she made the king and princes jealous of him.
Rabbah says pride goes before a fall, and Abaye and Rava say she prepared their feast with poison.
Cites Jeremiah 51:39 on preparing their feast.
Rabbah b. Abuha found Elijah and asked him.
Asks which of these reasons prompted Esther's action.
Elijah replies that it is all the reasons given by all the Tannaim and Amoraim.
Cites Esther 5:11 on Haman recounting his riches and the multitude of his children.
Asks how many the multitude of his children were.
Rav says ten died, ten were hanged, and ten went begging.
The Rabbis say those who went begging were seventy.
Cites 1 Samuel 2:5 with its word read as seventy.
Rami b. Abba says in all they were two hundred and eight.
R. Nahman b. Isaac explains the word is written defectively.
Cites Esther 6:1 that the sleep of the king was disturbed that night.
R. Tanhum says the sleep of the King of the Universe was disturbed; the Rabbis say those above and below.
Rava says it is literally the sleep of Ahasuerus.
A thought occurred to the king.
He asks what is the meaning of Esther inviting Haman.
He reasons that men conspire against him, or that someone he did not reward avoids telling him.
Cites Esther 6:1 that he ordered the book of records of the chronicles to be brought.
This teaches that they were read of themselves.
Cites the verse that it was found written.
Asks why it does not say a writing was found, and what this shows.

ranges.en: Shimshai erases while Gabriel writes; R. Shila's a fortiori: if an earthly record for Israel cannot be erased, a heavenly one cannot.
Cites Esther 6:3 that nothing was done for Mordecai.
Rava: they answered not from love of Mordecai but from hatred of Haman.
Cites Esther 6:4 that Haman had prepared a gallows for Mordecai.
A Tanna teaches that Haman prepared for himself, and then did so for Mordecai.
Haman asks who Mordecai is.
Cites Esther 6:10 where the answer is the Jew.
Haman says there are many Mordecais among the Jews.
Cites Esther 6:10 identifying him as the one sitting at the king's gate.
Haman says one village or river is enough; Ahasuerus orders that nothing fail of his words.
Cites Esther 6:11 that Haman took the clothes and the horse.
Haman finds Mordecai with the Rabbis, who flee; Mordecai prays while Haman waits until he finishes.
Haman asks what they were discussing.
Mordecai explains the handful of fine flour offered in the Temple to make atonement.
Haman says their handful displaced his ten thousand talents; Mordecai replies that a slave's property belongs to his master.
Haman urges Mordecai to put on the clothes and ride the horse the king desires.
Mordecai replies he must first bathe and trim his hair, as it is not proper to wear the king's garments unkempt.
Esther closed the baths and barbers' shops, so Haman himself washed and trimmed Mordecai's hair.
Mordecai asks Haman why he sighs.
Haman says the man honored above all nobles is now made a bath attendant and barber.
Mordecai retorts that Haman was a barber in Kefar Karzum for twenty-two years.
Haman washes and dresses Mordecai and tells him to mount.
Mordecai replies he is too weak from fasting to mount.
Haman stoops so Mordecai can mount, then kicks him.
Cites Proverbs 24:17 that one should not rejoice at an enemy's fall.
Mordecai replies that this applies to Israelites, while of you it is written in Deuteronomy 33:29.
Cites Deuteronomy 33:29 and Esther 6:11 on treading their high places and the king's honor.
Narrates Haman's daughter seeing her father on the horse and Mordecai walking, dumping a pot on him, and her death.
Cites Esther 6:12 that Mordecai returned to the king's gate.
R. Sheshet says Mordecai returned to sackcloth and fasting, and Haman mourned for his daughter.
Cites Esther 6:13 that Haman told Zeresh his wife and all his friends.
The text calls them friends and then wise men, so the wise are called wise.
R. Yohanan teaches that whoever says a wise thing even among the nations is called wise.
Haman's advisers reason that if Mordecai is from Judah or Benjamin they cannot prevail over him.
Cites Genesis 49:8 on Judah and Psalms 80:3 on Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh, plus Esther 6:13.
R. Yehuda b. Ila'i explains the two fallings: the nation is like dust and like stars.
Cites Esther 6:14 that the eunuchs came and hastened to bring Haman.
The word means they brought him in confusion.
Cites Esther 7:4 about being sold, and that the adversary is not worth the king's damage.
Esther replies that the adversary cares nothing for the king's loss, having killed Vashti and wanting to kill her.
Cites Esther 7:5 where the king spoke to Esther the queen.
Asks why the verb said appears twice.
R. Abbahu: he first spoke through an intermediary, and when she said she came from Saul's house he addressed her directly.
Cites Esther 7:6 that Esther said an adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman.
R. Elazar: she pointed at Ahasuerus, and an angel pushed her hand to point at Haman.
Cites Esther 7:7 on the king rising in anger and returning from the garden.
The king's return is compared to his rising, both done in anger.
The king finds angels as men uprooting trees, then Haman falls on the couch in his house.
Asks why the text says falling rather than had fallen.
R. Elazar: an angel came and made him fall on the couch.
Ahasuerus exclaims that trouble is inside and outside.
Cites Esther 7:8 and 7:9 on Haman and on Harbonah.
R. Elazar: Harbonah was wicked and part of the plot, and fled once it failed.
Cites Job 27:22 that he will flee from His hand.
Cites Esther 7:10 that the king's wrath abated.
Two assuagings: one of the King of the Universe and one of Ahasuerus, or of Esther and of Vashti.
Cites Genesis 45:22 that Benjamin was given five changes of clothing.
Asks whether it is possible that a righteous man would be made to suffer by this.

ranges.en: Asks how a man should fall into the very mistake he himself suffered from.
Rav's teaching: the two sela's of fine silk Jacob gave Joseph set off the descent to Egypt.
Benjamin b. Japhet: Jacob's gift hinted that a descendant would go out in five royal garments.
Cites Esther 8:15 on Mordecai going out in royal apparel, and Genesis 45:14 on Benjamin's neck.
Asks how many necks Benjamin had.
R. Elazar: Benjamin wept for the two Temples in his territory, and for Shiloh in Joseph's.
Cites Genesis 45:12 on the eyes of my brother Benjamin.
R. Elazar: Joseph bore no malice toward his brothers, as he bore none toward Benjamin.
Cites Genesis 45:23 on the ten donkeys laden with the good things of Egypt.
Asks what the good things of Egypt are.
Joseph sent old wine, which elderly men find comforting.
Cites Genesis 50:3 that his brothers also went and fell before him.
Proverb: a fox in its hour, bow down to it.
Asks how Joseph could be inferior to his brothers if compared to a fox.
The saying is applied to the case where Israel bowed on the bed's head.
Cites Genesis 47:31 on Israel bowing upon the bed's head.
R. Benjamin b. Japhet repeats the fox saying in R. Elazar's name.
Cites Genesis 50:21 that he comforted them and spoke to their heart.
R. Elazar: Joseph spoke words that would be acceptable to their hearts.
If ten lamps cannot extinguish one, how can one lamp extinguish ten?
Cites Esther 8:16 on the Jews having light, gladness, joy and honor.
Rav Judah: light means Torah.
Cites Proverbs 6:23 that the commandment is a lamp and the Torah a light.
Gladness means a festival day.
Cites Deuteronomy 16:14 that you shall be glad on your festival.
Joy means circumcision.
Cites Psalms 119:162 that I rejoice at your word.
Honor means tefillin.
Cites Deuteronomy 28:10 that all the peoples see the name of the Lord called upon you.
R. Eliezer the Great says this refers to the head tefillin.
Cites Esther 9:7 that Parshandata and the ten sons of Haman were slain.
R. Adda of Yaffo: the ten sons and the word ten are read in one breath, as they died in one breath.
R. Yohanan: the vav of vayzata must be drawn out like a boat-pole, since they were strung on one pole.
R. Shila: songs in Scripture are written as half bricks over whole bricks, with exceptions.
The exception is this song and the kings of Canaan, which are written differently.
Asks what the reason for the exception is.
So that they should never rise again from their downfall.
Cites Esther 9:12 that the king said the Jews have slain five hundred in Shushan.
R. Abbahu: an angel came and slapped him on the mouth.
Cites Esther 9:25 that when she came before the king he said along with the letter.
Asks why it says he said rather than she said.
R. Yohanan: she said that what is written should be said by word of mouth too.
R. Tanhum or R. Assi: the Megillah must be written on ruled lines, like the Torah.
Asks whether only the ordinance of Esther was upheld and not the words of the fasts.
R. Yohanan: both the fasts and the ordinance of Esther were upheld as Purim.
Cites Esther 9:32 on the ordinance of Esther.
Cites Esther 10:3 that Mordecai was accepted by most of his brothers, not all.
R. Joseph: study of Torah is greater than saving life, since Mordecai's rank changed in the lists.
Cites Ezra 2:2 and Nehemiah 7:7 on the lists of those who came with Zerubbabel.
Rabbah in R. Isaac b. Shmuel b. Marta's name: Torah is greater than building the Temple.
Rabbah in R. Isaac b. Shmuel b. Marta's name: Torah is greater than honoring parents, as Jacob was not punished in the Study House.

17a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why the years of Ishmael are counted in the Torah.
So that they can be used to reckon the years of Jacob.
Cites Genesis 25:17 on the years of Ishmael's life, 137.
Asks how much older Ishmael was than Isaac.
Fourteen years.
Cites Genesis 16:16, 21:5 and 25:26 for the ages of Abram, Abraham and Isaac at the births.
Asks how old Ishmael was when Jacob was born.
Jacob was seventy-four at birth, leaving Ishmael sixty-three more years.
A baraita: Jacob was sixty-three when blessed by his father, and Ishmael died around then.
Cites Genesis 28:6-9 on Esau taking Mahalath, daughter of Ishmael.
Asks why she needs to be called Ishmael's daughter if she is known to be Nevayot's sister.
Ishmael betrothed her and then died, so Nevayot her brother gave her in marriage.
Adds the years: sixty-three plus fourteen gives seventy-seven at Joseph's birth.
Cites Genesis 41:46 that Joseph was thirty when he stood before Pharaoh.
Adds seven years of plenty and two of famine, giving a hundred and sixteen.
Cites Genesis 47:8-9 where Jacob says his years of wandering are a hundred and thirty.
Rather, the fourteen years in the House of Ever were not counted.
A baraita: Jacob was hidden fourteen years in the House of Ever, and Ever died two years after Jacob went to Aram Naharaim.
Asks how we know Jacob was not punished for those fourteen years.
A baraita: Joseph was away from his father twenty-two years; the fourteen years in Ever's house are not counted.
Jacob's time at Laban's was twenty years because he spent two years on the way.
A baraita: Jacob left Aram Naharaim and spent eighteen months at Sukkot.
Cites Genesis 33:17 that Jacob journeyed to Sukkot, built a house, and spent six months at Bethel.
Mishnah: the chapter on reading the Megillah; reading out of order, in translation, or with breaks, and on what writing materials are valid.
Rava derives from Esther 9:27 that just as the time cannot be reversed, neither can the order of the writing.
Asks whether the verse speaks of reading, since keeping is written there.
It speaks of keeping, as written in Esther 9:28 about keeping these two days.
Cites Esther 9:28 that these days shall be remembered and kept.
Remembering is compared to keeping, so it too cannot be done out of order.
A Tanna teaches the same rule applies to Hallel, the Shema recitation and the Amidah.
Asks from where the rule for Hallel is derived.
Rabbah cites Psalms 113:3 from the rising of the sun to its setting.
R. Joseph cites Psalms 118:24, this is the day the Lord has made.
R. Avia cites Psalms 113:2, let the name of the Lord be blessed.
R. Nahman b. Isaac, or R. Aha b. Jacob, cites Psalms 113:2, from this time forth and forever.
A baraita: the Shema must be recited as written, in Rabbi's view, and the Sages say any language.
Asks what is Rabbi's reason.
Scripture says it, so Rabbi holds it must be read as written.

17b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites Deuteronomy 6:6 that these words shall be in their form.
Asks what the reason of the Sages is.
Because Scripture says hear, meaning in any language you understand.
Asks whether Rabbi too must derive from the word hear.
Hear requires that the ear hear what the mouth says.
The Sages accept that one who recites the Shema without hearing it with his ears has fulfilled his duty.
Asks whether the Sages too need and they shall be to teach order.
It teaches that the Shema must not be recited backward.
Asks from where Rabbi derives the rule against reciting backward.
The Sages do not distinguish between words and the words.
