Asks whether Rabbi holds the whole Torah may be recited in any language.
Had the whole Torah been Hebrew only, and they shall be would be needless, so it was written for the Sages' view.
Asks whether the Sages hold the whole Torah is in Hebrew only.
Hear was needed, since it might be read as Rabbi's and they shall be, so God wrote hear.
Asks from where we know the Amidah prayer.
A baraita: Shimon Hapakuli arranged the eighteen blessings before Rabban Gamaliel at Yavneh; others say a hundred and twenty elders did.
Asks from where we know to say the blessing of the fathers.
Cites Psalms 29:1 to ascribe to the Lord the sons of the mighty.
Asks from where we know to say the blessing of mighty deeds.
Cites Psalms 29:1 to ascribe glory and strength to the Lord.
Asks from where we know to say the sanctifications.
Cites Psalms 29:2 to ascribe glory due to his name and worship in holy beauty.
Asks why understanding is said after holiness.
Cites Isaiah 29:23-24 on sanctifying the Holy One of Jacob, and those who err in spirit reaching understanding.
Asks why repentance is said after understanding.
Cites Isaiah 6:10 on understanding with the heart, repenting and being healed.
Asks why healing is not said right after repentance.
Do not think so, since Isaiah 55:7 places return and compassion before forgiveness.
Asks what led the Gemara to rely on that verse.
Cites Psalms 103:3-4 on forgiveness, healing, and redemption from the pit.
This implies redemption and healing come after forgiveness.
Asks how that squares with the verse that he will repent and be healed.
That healing is the healing of forgiveness, not of sickness.
Asks why redemption is said in the seventh blessing.
Rava: redemption is in the seventh year, and war in the seventh is the beginning of redemption.
Asks why healing is said in the eighth blessing.
R. Aha: circumcision requires healing and is done on the eighth day.
Asks why the blessing of the years is said in the ninth.
R. Alexandri: it is against those who raise prices, as Psalms 10:15 says.
Asks why the gathering of exiles follows the blessing of the years.
Cites Ezekiel 36:8 that Israel's branches shall yield fruit as the exiles come.
When the exiles are gathered, judgment falls on the wicked.
Cites Isaiah 1:25-26 on purging dross and restoring judges.
When judgment falls on the wicked, the transgressors cease, and presumptuous sinners are included with them.
Cites Isaiah 1:28 that transgressors and sinners are destroyed together.
When transgressors are gone, the horn of the righteous is exalted.
Cites Psalms 75:11 that all the horns of the wicked will be cut off.
Righteous converts are included with the righteous.
Cites Leviticus 19:32 on honoring the aged and the stranger who sojourns with you.
Asks where the horn of the righteous is exalted.
Cites Psalms 122:6 on praying for the peace of Jerusalem.
When Jerusalem is built, David will come.

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites Hosea 3:5 that Israel will return and seek the Lord and David their king.
When David comes, prayer will come.
Cites Isaiah 56:7 on bringing them to my holy mountain and house of prayer.
When prayer has come, the Temple service will come.
Cites Isaiah 56:7 on burnt-offerings and sacrifices accepted on my altar.
When the service has come, thanksgiving will come.
Cites Psalms 50:23 that whoever offers thanksgiving honors me.
Asks why the priestly blessing is said after thanksgiving.
Cites Leviticus 9:22 on Aaron blessing the people after the offerings.
Asks whether it could be said before the service.
No, since the verse says he came down from offering, not to offer.
Asks why it is not said after the service instead.
No, since the verse says whoever offers thanksgiving.
Asks what reason there is to rely on that verse rather than the other.
Worship and thanksgiving are one matter.
Asks why give peace is said after the priestly blessing.
Cites Numbers 6:27 and Psalms 29:11 that the blessing of the Holy One is peace.
Asks why Shimon the Pakulite arranged the prayers if the elders had already done so.
They had forgotten them, and he went back and arranged them.
Beyond this it is forbidden to declare the praises of the Holy One, as R. Elazar teaches.
Cites Psalms 106:2 on who can express the mighty acts of the Lord.
R. Yohanan: one who tells the praises of the Holy One in excess is uprooted from the world.
Cites Job 37:20 on whether a man who speaks shall be swallowed.
R. Judah of Kefar Gibboraya expounds on silence as praise, citing Psalms 65:2.
Cites Psalms 65:2 that silence is praise for You.
The cure for everything is silence.
R. Dimi reports the Western saying that a word is worth a sela and silence two.
Mishnah: one who read the Megillah by heart has not fulfilled the obligation.
Rava derives from the shared word zikaron in Esther 9:28 and Exodus 17:14 that it must be in a book.
Asks how we know this remembrance means reading aloud, and not reading with the eyes.
Deuteronomy 25:17 teaches remember with the mouth, since forgetting in the heart is already stated.
Mishnah: one who read the Megillah in translation has not fulfilled the obligation.
Asks what the case of reading in translation actually is.
It is needed only where the text was written in translation and read in translation.
Mishnah: one may read it to those who do not know Hebrew in the vernacular.
Asks how this agrees with the Mishnah saying reading in any language does not fulfill.
Rav and Shmuel both say the Greek vernacular.
Asks what that means if it was written in Hebrew and read in Greek.
R. Aha in R. Elazar's name: it refers to a text written in Greek.
R. Aha in R. Elazar's name: God called Jacob El, as Genesis 33:20 shows.
Cites Genesis 33:20 that the God of Israel called him El.
The verb refers to God calling Jacob El, not Jacob calling the altar El.
Objects with a baraita listing Coptic, Hebrew, Elamite, Median and Greek as not fulfilling.
That baraita means reading in each people's own language.
Asks why Rav and Shmuel explain the Mishnah as Greek rather than any vernacular.
The Mishnah agrees with the baraita, and Rav and Shmuel meant that Greek is good for all.
Asks how Greek for Greeks and not for others squares with their ruling.
Rabban Shimon b. Gamaliel says when other languages were permitted for scrolls, only Greek was.
Asks whether they should simply say the halakhah follows Rabban Shimon b. Gamaliel.
Had they said so, one might limit it to other books, but the Megillah says according to their writing.
Mishnah: one who does not know Hebrew but hears it read in Hebrew has fulfilled his obligation.
Asks how that person fulfills, not knowing what is said.
He is like women and amei haaretz who hear without understanding.
Ravina objects: do we know the meaning of ha-ahashteranim, and yet we fulfill by proclaiming the miracle?
Mishnah: one who read with interruptions has fulfilled his obligation.
The Rabbis did not know serugin until they heard Rabbi's maidservant speak to visitors entering in intervals.
The Rabbis did not know haluglugot until they heard Rabbi's maidservant speak to a man peeling purslane.
The Rabbis did not know salseleah until they heard a maidservant speaking to a man curling his hair.
Rabbah b. Bar Hana did not know yehav until an Arab asked him to lift his yehav onto a camel.
The Rabbis did not know ta'atitah until they heard a maidservant tell her friend to sweep with the broom.
Our Rabbis taught: one who reads it with breaks has fulfilled his obligation.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: if one reads with omissions, he has not fulfilled his obligation.
R. Muna in R. Judah's name: even with breaks, if he pauses long enough to finish, he must start again.
R. Joseph rules that the halakhah follows R. Muna in R. Judah's name.
Abaye asks whether finishing the whole means from where he stopped or from the beginning.
R. Joseph: from the beginning to the end, otherwise there would be no fixed standard.
Versions differ between Sura and Pumbedita on whether Rav and Shmuel accept R. Muna's ruling.
R. Joseph: accept R. Bibi's version, since Shmuel follows a minority view, citing the yavam mishnah of R. Judah b. Batera.
Shmuel says the halakhah follows R. Judah b. Batera.
A baraita: if a scribe omitted letters or verses and the reader read them as a translator would, he has fulfilled his obligation.
Objects with a baraita that a torn or rubbed scroll is invalid, resolved by partial versus full damage.
A baraita: if a reader omitted a verse, or joined a congregation midway, he must read from the beginning to the end.
Mishnah: one who napped has fulfilled his obligation.
Asks what napping means.
R. Ashi: he sleeps and is not truly asleep, is awake but not fully, and responds only when reminded.
Mishnah: one who wrote, expounded, or corrected it fulfills if he directed his heart.
Asks how writing could be done without fulfilling if he merely arranges verses by heart.
Rather he writes each verse and then recites it.
Asks whether he fulfills, since R. Helbo says the whole must already be written.
Rather a Megillah lies before him and he reads from it verse by verse and writes.
Asks whether this supports Rabbah b. Bar Hanah's ban on writing without a copy, or whether it was a case of a copy at hand.
Rabbah b. Bar Hanah in R. Yohanan's name: one may not write a letter without a copy.
Objects with a baraita that R. Meir wrote out a Megillah from memory when none was at hand.
R. Abbahu: R. Meir is different, as Proverbs 4:25 applies to him.
Rami b. Hama asks R. Jeremiah what the verse about the eyes means.
It refers to the words of Torah that one's eyes cannot skim over, so R. Meir produced correctly.
R. Hisda found R. Hananel writing scrolls without a copy and rebuked him.
The Sages ruled one may not write a letter without a copy, though the whole Torah could be written from memory.
Objects that R. Meir did write a Megillah from memory.
In an emergency the rule is different.
Abaye permitted Bar Habu's household to write tefillin and mezuzot without a copy.
Asks whose authority Abaye followed.
A baraita: R. Jeremiah says tefillin and mezuzot may be written without a copy and need no ruled lines.
The law: tefillin need no lines, mezuzot do, and both may be written without a copy because they are frequently recited.
Mishnah: if the Megillah was written in sam, the sam is to be understood.
Explains sam as arsenic and sekarta as red chalk or vermilion, and kumus as gum.

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Glosses the materials: kankantum is sandler's blacking, diftera is salted skin, neyar is paper.
A Megillah is valid only if written in Hebrew square script.
Cites Esther 9:27 with the words according to their writing.
Mishnah: the Megillah is valid only if written on parchment, in ink.
Asks from where the rule of parchment and ink is derived.
Derives it from the word writing in Esther 9:29 and Jeremiah 36:18 about writing with ink.
Mishnah: a townsman visiting a walled city reads by the local custom if he returns home, otherwise with the locals.
Asks from where a person reads the Megillah and fulfills his obligation.
Mishnah: R. Meir says all of it, R. Judah from There was a Jew, R. Yose from After these things.
Rava: this applies only if he intends to return on the night of the fourteenth.
Asks Rava from where he derives this ruling.
Cites Esther 9:19 on the Jews of the villages dwelling in unwalled towns.
A villager for one day is called a villager, so a walled-city dweller for one day is called one.
Rava: a villager who goes to a town reads with the rest, because the Rabbis conceded for the villagers.
Asks what the reason for this is.
The villager should read with the townspeople, but the concession applies only while he is in his own place.
Abaye objects that a walled-city dweller who goes to a town should read by his own custom, and the text was emended.
Baraita: R. Shimon b. Yohai says from On that night, and R. Yohanan says they all derived from one verse.
Cites Esther 9:29 that Esther and Mordecai wrote all the power of the letter.
Interpretations: the power refers to Ahasuerus, Mordecai, Haman or the miracle, and R. Huna cites Esther 9:26.
Whoever reads the whole Megillah explains the verses as Ahasuerus using the Temple vessels and killing Vashti.
Whoever reads from There was a Jew explains Mordecai's act of refusing idolatry and the miracle that followed.
Whoever reads from After these things explains Haman's envy at Mordecai not bowing and their hanging.
Whoever reads from On that night explains Ahasuerus bringing the Chronicles after Esther invited Haman.
R. Helbo in R. Hama b. Guria's name in Rav's name: the halakhah follows the view that the whole Megillah must be written.
Rav: the Megillah is called book and letter, so flax thread is invalid but sinew threads are valid if evenly spaced.
R. Judah in Shmuel's name: reading from a Megillah among the Writings is invalid, while Rava limits this to a substantial difference in length.
Levi b. Samuel read a Megillah before R. Judah, Rav's pupil.

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Quoted teaching that reading the Megillah written among the Writings does not discharge the obligation.
R. Hiyya b. Abba reports R. Yohanan ruling that such a reading in a public setting fails.
Objection that the ruling was only about public reading, and the statement was taught in that context.
R. Yohanan holds that the unstitched space in a Torah scroll is a halakhah given to Moses at Sinai.
Objection that the space was prescribed only so that the scroll would not tear.
R. Yohanan says a hole the size of a needle eye would have been too bright for Moses and Elijah.
Verse from Exodus cited: no person may see God and live.
Introduces R. Yohanan teaching about what God showed Moses at the mountain.
Asks what the verse about the words written on the tablets is meant to teach.
The verse teaches that Moses was shown the fine details of Torah and the later innovations of the Scribes.
Asks what those Scribal innovations actually were.
The innovation is the public reading of the Megillah.
Mishnah: everyone may read the Megillah except a deaf person, an imbecile and a minor; R. Judah validates a minor.
Asks which Tanna holds that a deaf reader does not discharge the obligation even after the fact.
R. Matanah says the Mishnah follows R. Yose.
Mishnah on the Shema case: one who did not let it be heard by his own ears has fulfilled, but R. Yose disagrees.
Asks whether the Mishnah might follow R. Judah instead, so that only ab initio reading is barred.
Rejects that reading: the deaf is grouped with the imbecile and minor, and the Mishnah may instead be all R. Judah.
Proposed corrected wording of the Mishnah, listing the deaf, imbecile and minor as exclusions.
Explains that the minor who is not yet educated is excluded, while an educated minor is valid even ab initio.
Asks how the first clause of the Mishnah has been explained.
It is explained as R. Judah's view, valid only after the fact.
Baraita from R. Judah son of R. Shimon b. Pazzi: a deaf person who speaks may set aside terumah ab initio.
Asks whose view that baraita states and whether R. Judah would allow even ab initio.
Baraita: one should not recite birkat hamazon silently, but if he did, he has fulfilled it.
Asks whose opinion that baraita represents.
It is neither R. Judah nor R. Yose; each would give a different ruling, so the baraita is unresolved.

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Resolves the difficulty: the first view is R. Judah's own, the second his teacher's, so both are consistent.
R. Judah's baraita in the name of R. Elazar b. Azariah: the Shema must be audible to the reciter, citing Deuteronomy.
R. Meir holds that the Shema verse requires directing the heart's intention, derived from Deuteronomy.
Concludes that R. Judah agreed with his teacher, and the baraita of Yehuda son of Shimon b. Pazzi follows R. Meir.
R. Judah validates a minor for reading the Megillah.
Anecdotes: R. Judah and Rabbi read as minors and were told a minor's testimony cannot serve as proof.
Asks why the objectors did not simply say that proof cannot come from a minor.
They gave two replies: you were a minor, and even as an adult proof cannot come from one who permits it.
Mishnah: no Megillah reading, circumcision, immersion or sprinkling on the relevant days; done after dawn they are valid.
Source for the rule that the Megillah is read by day, drawn from the verse in Esther.
Objection: this would refute R. Yehoshua b. Levi, who required reading by night and again by day.
Reply: the Mishnah's wording refers only to the day.
Mishnah rules on circumcision and immersion or sprinkling supported by verses from Leviticus and Numbers.
Mishnah rule that a woman keeping day for day must not immerse until sunrise.
Asks why the woman keeping day for day is singled out, since she would seem to match all immersion obligations.
Explains why the rule is needed: lest she be likened to the zav's case, and the verse shows she must still count day for day.

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates that counting is done by day, and that acts performed after dawn are valid.
Rava derives from the Genesis creation verse that a gradually lightening period counts as day.
Objection: by that logic darkness would be night only after the stars appear, which conflicts with the derivation.
R. Zera derives the same point from the Nehemiah verse about working from dawn until the stars appear.
Asks what the purpose of the second quotation is.
Hypothesis: the period from dawn to sunset is not really day, so the verse must be read differently.
Come and hear: the Nehemiah verse about night guard and day work is cited as support.
Mishnah listing the rites valid all day and those valid all night, with the general principle stated at the end.
Source verses: Esther for reading the Megillah by day, and Psalms for the Hallel.
Verses from Leviticus and Numbers establish daytime for taking the lulav and blowing the shofar.
Verse from Leviticus supports the musaf offerings by day, and the musaf prayer was modeled on them.
Confession over the oxen is derived by analogy to Yom Kippur atonement, which is performed by day.
Deuteronomy verses support the daytime confession over the tithe.
Verses from Leviticus and Numbers support daytime laying on of hands, slaughter and waving the omer.
Numbers and Leviticus verses, plus an analogy to waving, support daytime bringing near, pinching and sprinkling.
Sotah drink is derived from a repeated word Torah, linking the two verses as a verbal analogy.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Analogy: just as judgment is done by day, the rite here must also be done by day.
Rabbi Yannai's school: the heifer's neck-breaking and metzora purification follow sacrificial and daytime rules, supported by Leviticus.
A master's rule: the whole night is valid for omer harvesting, with counting at night and bringing by day, and fat and limbs burned at night.
Verse from Leviticus: the burning of fat and limbs continues through the whole night until morning.
General principle: any matter whose commandment is by day is valid all day.
Asks what the general principle is meant to include.
It includes arranging and removing the frankincense dishes, in line with R. Yose.
Baraita of R. Yose: removing the old showbread in the morning and setting the new one in the evening is acceptable.
Asks how the obligation of the verse about the table before God is fulfilled.
The table must never be left without bread.
Any matter whose commandment is at night is valid all night.
Asks what this night rule is meant to include.
It includes eating the Passover offering, against the view of R. Eleazar b. Azariah.
Baraita and verse argument that the Passover night-eating runs only until midnight, by analogy to the Exodus verse.
Chapter-ending formula introducing the next chapter.
Mishnah on Megillah reading standing or sitting, by one or two readers, and how many read from the Torah on weekdays and Shabbat minchah.
Mishnah: four read on Rosh Chodesh and intermediate days, with numbers for festivals, Yom Kippur and Shabbat, and blessing and haftarah rules.
A Tanna teaches that this numbering rule does not apply to the public reading of the Torah.
Asks from where this distinction for Torah reading is derived.
R. Abbahu cites Deuteronomy: the verse stand here with me, meaning the Torah reader stands.
R. Abbahu adds that were it not written, one could not say it: the Holy One also stood.
Asks how we know a teacher should not sit on a couch while students sit on the ground.
The verse stand here with me is cited as the source that the teacher should stand, not sit.
Baraita: Torah was learned standing from Moses until Rabban Gamliel, then sitting, and the honor of Torah was diminished.
Two verses about Moses on the mountain, one saying he sat and one saying he stood, seem to conflict.
Rav: standing to learn, sitting to review. R. Hanina: stooping. R. Yohanan: sitting means staying. Rava: easy material standing, hard sitting.
Mishnah conclusion: whether one or two read the Megillah, they have fulfilled the obligation.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Tanna's baraita on public reading: for Torah one reads and one translates; for Hallel and the Megillah even ten may read.
Asks what the reason is for allowing so many readers for Hallel and the Megillah.
Because people cherish these readings, they pay attention and listen.
Blessing is said before the reading where it is customary; Abaye adds that before the reading a blessing is a mitzvah.
Asks what the word passing in the Shmuel teaching is meant to imply.
Verses from Samuel, Genesis and Micah are cited to show that passing means before.
Asks what blessing is said before reading the Megillah.
Rav Sheshet, visiting Rav Ashi, recited a blessing ending with the abbreviation for the formula.
Asks what exactly the blessing says.
Gives the text of the blessing: God who fights our fight, judges our judgment and avenges us.
Rava's ending is the God who saves; R. Papa says both endings should be said, and three read on Monday, Thursday and Shabbat minchah.
Asks what the three readers represent.
R. Assi: Torah, Prophets and Writings. Rava: priests, Levites and Israelites.
Asks what the ten verses required in synagogue, including the opening verse, represent.
Four views: ten idle men of the synagogue, the Ten Commandments, David's ten praises, and the ten sayings of creation.
Asks what the ten creative statements are, since only nine are obvious.
Counting the opening word as a creative statement, supported by Psalms.
Rava: the first reader who reads four verses is praiseworthy, and likewise the second and third.
Mishnah on the three baskets, the lamps and the middle reader, cited as support for praising the first, middle and last readers.
The last reader is praised by the rule that holy matters go up but not down; the sources state the four-verse rule and the Rosh Chodesh and Hol Hamoed reading.
Ulla asks Rava how the Rosh Chodesh portion is read.
The Rosh Chodesh portion from Numbers has eight verses.
Asks how the eight verses should be divided among the readers.
Objection: two readers of three verses each leaves two verses over, and four each leaves too few for the final section.
Counts for Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh: two verses for Shabbat and five for the new month.
Asks whether two verses may be read from one portion and one from the next.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rule: one may not begin a section with fewer than three verses.
Proposes splitting the verses two and three across readers, which would leave only two verses.
The reply: no direct ruling is known, but a similar rule about the Sunday reading of Genesis divisions.
Objection: how can the two-reader portion of Genesis have only five verses, given the rule that a reader must read at least three.
Rav holds the reader repeats the verse, while Shmuel holds he may divide it; each gives his reasoning.
Objection to Shmuel from R. Hananiah's report that R. Hanina permitted verse division only for schoolchildren.
Asks what the reason was in that case.
It was unavoidable there, and it is equally unavoidable here.
Shmuel holds that he divides the verse.
Asks why Shmuel did not say the reader repeats instead.
Repetition is forbidden as a decree against error by those coming in and going out of the synagogue.
Baraita objection against both views: a section of six verses is read by two, and the first reader's remainder must be divided.
Asks whether, on that premise, each view should apply its own remedy here.
That case differs because the remedy is possible there.
R. Tanhum in the name of R. Joshua b. Levi: the halakhah follows the others, and a section's end likewise must not leave fewer than three verses.
Dismisses the parallel as obvious, arguing that a stricter view on the beginning implies strictness at the end too.
Asks what the concern would be if one did not know the rule.
People entering are common, while those leaving the Torah reading are uncommon, so the rule is stated explicitly.
Asks why the first Tanna bars leaving a short remainder, and why the same concern does not apply to entering.
A person entering asks how much has already been read, so no decree is needed.
Rabbah son of Raba asks R. Joseph what the law is.
The verse is repeated, and a middle reader is the one who repeats.
General rule: wherever there is an additional offering, the reading follows the set counts.
Asks how many read on a public fast, and whether a public fast counts as having an additional prayer.
Mishnah cited: four read on New Moons and intermediate festival days, and three on Monday, Thursday and Shabbat minchah.
Rejects the proof: nothing conclusive can be learned from that Mishnah about public fasts.
Story of Rav in Babylon during a public fast, cited as evidence about how many read and blessings.
Asks why Rav did not bless after reading, if he read as a layman and another was to read after him.
Rav read as a kohen, as R. Huna did too.
Asks how R. Huna could read as kohen when Shmuel, also a kohen, was senior to Rav.
Shmuel was subject to Rav, and Rav honored him only in his presence.
Reasoning: Rav read as a kohen, since a blessing before reading implies that he was a kohen.
Asks why Rav blessed before reading but not after, and whether he should bless after too.
It is different where Rav was present to read, since the others were entering.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: They do not leave the reading during the Torah reading, which concludes the preceding discussion.
Come and hear: days when work is restricted, such as public fasts, have three readers, while Rosh Hodesh and intermediate days have four.
R. Ashi objects that this is not how the Mishnah is taught, and asks what the general rule would include if not public fasts and Tisha B'Av.
Asks, on R. Ashi's reading, whose view the Mishnah represents.
Baraita on Tisha B'Av falling on Monday, Tuesday or Thursday, giving the views of the first Tanna and R. Yose.
Objection: the phrase this is the general rule then seems problematic.
No: the general rule includes Rosh Hodesh and the intermediate days of the festival.
Objection: the Mishnah states Rosh Hodesh and intermediate days explicitly, so they need not be included in the general rule.
The Mishnah gives a sign that festivals and intermediate days differ, and the general principle is that each added distinguishing feature adds a reader.
Applying the principle: four read on Rosh Hodesh and intermediate days with an additional offering, five on festivals, six on Yom Kippur and seven on Shabbat.
Recounts the story of Rav in Babylon during a public fast, who read, blessed on starting, and did not fall on his face.
Asks why Rav did not fall on his face when the congregation did.
There was a stone pavement there, so falling on the face was not appropriate.
Baraita on Leviticus about figured stone: the prohibition is only on the stone pavement, as Ulla held.
Asks why only Rav is mentioned, when the rest of the congregation would also have acted this way.
Rav was in front of the congregation and did not want to trouble them; alternatively he spread hands and feet, following Ulla's view.
Asks why Rav did not simply fall on his face without spreading his limbs.
He did not want to change his custom. Alternatively, an important man may fall on his face only if answered, as Joshua was.
Baraita defines kidah as falling on the face, keriah as kneeling, and hishtahavayah as spreading hands and feet; Levi performed kidah before Rabbi and became lame.
Asks whether the lameness really resulted from that act, given that one should not speak against Heaven.
Both things caused it: the act and the words against Heaven.
Hiyya b. Abin reports seeing Abaye and Rava leaning over in the same posture.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Anecdote about Rava at prayer, then the Mishnah's counts: five readers on festivals, six on Yom Kippur, and so on.
Asks whose view the Mishnah follows.
It is neither R. Ishmael nor R. Akiva, as a baraita gives each view on the readers' numbers and whether they may be increased.
Objection: following either Tanna creates a conflict over the number of additional readers or over six versus seven.
Rava: the Mishnah follows the school of R. Ishmael, whose baraita gives five, six and seven and allows only increases.
Objection: this would make R. Ishmael contradict himself, so two Tannaim must be reporting in his name.
Asks which Tanna taught the baraita on how early people come to and leave synagogue on festivals, Yom Kippur and Shabbat.
Baraita on the timing of arriving and leaving synagogue on each day, cited as evidence for the reader counts.
Resolves the proof: it may be R. Akiva who adds a reader, or R. Ishmael, whose service is long.
Asks what the numbers three, five and seven represent.
Amoraim disagree: one links the numbers to the priestly blessing and the other to the door-keepers and those who saw the king's face.
R. Joseph taught the three, five and seven as the door-keepers and those who saw the king's face, in the same order.
Abaye asks why this was not explained earlier; R. Joseph replies he did not know Abaye wanted it.
Jacob the Min asks R. Judah what the six of Yom Kippur represent.
R. Judah: the six at Ezra's right and six at his left, citing the Nehemiah verse naming the men on the platform.
Objection: the named men add up to seven, not six, so the count does not fit.
Zechariah and Meshullam are one person, and he was called Meshullam because he was perfect in his deeds.
Baraita: anyone may be counted among the seven readers, even a minor or a woman, though the Sages barred women from reading the Torah out of respect for the congregation.
Asks whether the maftir reader counts among the seven.
R. Huna and R. Jeremiah b. Abba disagree; the one who says he does not count follows Ulla, who holds the haftarah reader reads only out of respect for the Torah.
Objection: a baraita requires twenty-one verses for the haftarah, which would be twenty-four if the maftir reader counted.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The haftarah need not correspond in verse count to the Torah reading.
Rava objects: the haftarah of Jeremiah has fewer than twenty-one verses and is still read, so the rule seems inconsistent.
R. Shmuel b. Abba's anecdote about R. Yohanan stopping early, and R. Tahlifa's distinction: where there is a translator, one may stop earlier.

Mishnah listing what is not done without a quorum: Shema, passing before the ark, priestly blessing, Torah reading, haftarah, mourning and wedding blessings, and naming God in Birkat Hamazon, all requiring ten.
Asks from where the quorum rule for sanctification is derived.
R. Hiyya b. Abba in the name of R. Yohanan derives the ten-person quorum from the verse about being sanctified among Israel, linked by analogy to the word congregation.
Mishnah clause: no stops at funerals and no standing or sitting rites with fewer than ten.
Reason: when one must say stand and sit, it is improper to do so with fewer than ten, as it is inappropriate for so few to be called dear friends.
Mishnah clause: no blessing for mourners or bridegrooms without a quorum.
Asks what the blessing of mourners is.
R. Yitzchak in the name of R. Yohanan: the mourners' blessing is said in the public square with ten present, and the mourners are not counted.
Mishnah clause: no naming God in the Birkat Hamazon invitation with fewer than ten.
Reason: the inviter must say let us bless our God, which is improper with fewer than ten.
Mishnah clause: for redeeming sanctified land nine and a priest suffice, and similarly for people.
Asks from where Shmuel's reading of this mishnah is derived.
Shmuel: the ten priests in the passage, one needed for the priest and the rest as a limitation after a limitation, add up to nine Israelites and one priest.
Objection: why not read five priests and five Israelites instead, which would be a difficulty.
Asks how a human being can be sanctified, given the mishnah's comparison.
R. Abbahu: this refers to one who vows his monetary value, which is estimated like a slave, and a slave is compared to property.
Mishnah: one reading the Torah publicly may not read fewer than three verses, nor read more than one verse at a time to the translator.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah rule: in a prophetic reading one may read three verses at once and skip ahead, but not in the Torah, and only so far as the translator does not stop.
Asks what the three verses of the prophet correspond to.
R. Assi: they correspond to Torah, Prophets and Writings.
Repeats the rule that one reads one verse at a time to the translator from Torah, three from a prophet, and skipping is allowed in a prophet but not in the Torah; illustrated from Isaiah 52.
Objection: the High Priest's Yom Kippur reading of Leviticus appears to skip within the Torah, contrary to the rule.
Abaye: no contradiction; the cases differ in whether the translator has already stopped before the place is found.
Objection: the baraita says skipping in a prophet is allowed, implying the Torah rule is a general one.
Abaye: the rule for the Torah is about one subject, and the other case about two subjects; a baraita confirms this.
Baraita on skipping between prophets, and the Mishnah on who may lead the haftarah, the Shema and the ark, including minors, the poor, and the blind.
Asks the reason for these restrictions.
Rav Papa: for honor. Rabbah bar Shimi: to avoid quarrels.
Asks what practical difference lies between these two reasons.
The difference shows in the case of one who reads without pay.
Objection: if the reason is avoiding quarrels, why would a child, who would not quarrel, be barred from passing before the ark for his father or teacher?
The reason is respect for the child's father and teacher, not the child himself.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Quarrel concerns also apply here, and a person in rags may publicly recite the Shema, as taught.
Ulla b. Rav asks Abaye whether a child in rags may read in the Torah.
Abaye: compare the naked person, who is barred out of respect for the congregation; the same respect applies here.
Mishnah: a blind man may publicly recite the Shema.
Objection: R. Judah was told that many who expounded the Chariot had never seen it, so the blind can also expound.
R. Judah: in that case all depends on the mind, but the blind man's reading needs light, which he does not get.
Objection: the reading is for benefit from light, and the blind derive none, so the rabbis would also disagree.
The rabbis hold that the blind do derive benefit, following R. Yose.
R. Yose was troubled by the verse about groping at noon, and recounts meeting a blind man carrying a torch so people would see and save him.
Mishnah: a priest with deformed hands may not lift his hands for the blessing, and R. Judah extends this to discolored hands.
Gemara: deformities that disqualify include spotted, curved or bent hands, and priests from Haifa, Beth Shean or Tivonim who mispronounce letters.
Anecdote: R. Hiyya tells R. Shimon b. Rabbi that a thick voice disqualifies a Levite from singing on the platform, and the reply uses the verse about waiting.
R. Huna: a man whose eyes run may not lift his hands.
Objection: someone near R. Huna spread his hands, so the rule must allow exceptions.
Baraita: a man whose eyes run may not lift his hands, but he is permitted if the townspeople are accustomed to him.
R. Yohanan: a blind person in even one eye may not lift his hands.
Objection: someone near R. Yohanan spread his hands, which seems to contradict the rule.
Baraita: the blind in one eye may not lift his hands, but are permitted if the townspeople are used to them.
R. Judah: discolored hands bar the priestly blessing, but a community whose main occupation is that is permitted.
Mishnah: one who says he will not pass before the ark in colored clothing or in shoes, and the rules on tefillin, which must be square, not round.
Asks the reason for barring the person with round tefillin from leading prayer.
We suspect some heresy has been implanted in him.
Mishnah repeated: one who makes his tefillin round is in danger and has no religious value.
Asks whether this Mishnah is already the baraita on square tefillin as a law from Sinai.
Baraita: square tefillin is a law from Moses at Sinai.
Rava: the square shape refers to the stitching and diagonal; R. Papa: the Mishnah concerns tefillin round as a nut.
Opening of the next Mishnah on one who says a vow.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: blessings that sound like heresy, such as thanking twice or speaking of a nest of a bird, and euphemisms in the forbidden-marriage passage, are silenced.
Explains why the phrases are restricted: they imply two powers, or that God's goodness is conditional on the good alone.
A Mishnah teaches that one must bless God for evil as for good, which tells against a blessing specifically for a nest.
Asks why the amoraim disagreed about the nest blessing.
Two Palestinian amoraim give opposed reasons: jealousy of creation, or mistaking God's decrees for acts of mercy.
Anecdote: a man before the ark in Rabbah's presence asks for mercy on us in the same words as the nest blessing.
Rabbah praises the man's skill at pleasing his Master.
Abaye objects that the man should have been silenced, as the Mishnah teaches, and Rabbah only wanted to sharpen Abaye.
Anecdote: a man before the ark before R. Hanina recites a long list of divine praises.
R. Hanina objects that only the first three praises are established by Moses and the Men of the Great Assembly, and the rest is excessive, like praising a rich man for a thousand.
R. Hanina: everything is in heaven's hands except the fear of heaven, citing Deuteronomy.
Fear of heaven is a small matter for Moses, as a person asked for a large vessel does not find it hard, but a small one feels big.
Zera: one who says Hear, Hear is like one who says we give thanks twice.
Objection: one who repeats the Shema is disgraceful, though not silenced, which seems to contradict the earlier rule.
Resolution: one repeats each word in one case and a whole sentence in the other.
Papa asks whether repetition may come from improper intention at first, now corrected.
Rava: one must not treat heaven like a friend; if intention is lacking, one should be struck until it is present.
Mishnah on euphemisms for parents' shame, with Joseph's teaching of the example.
School of R. Ishmael: the verse about giving seed refers to an Israelite who fathers a child by a Gentile woman for idolatry.
Mishnah on which portions are read and translated, read without translation, or neither, and the disputes over the haftarah of the chariot and of Jerusalem's abominations.
Gemara: the Tanna distinguishes portions read and translated, read only, or neither, with a mnemonic list.
The account of creation is read and translated.
Asks what one might think, namely that people might ask about what is above and what is below.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that the teaching covers what precedes and follows, so the stated list is complete.
The story of Lot and his daughters is read and translated.
Asks why the obvious case needs stating, and what concern might arise.
It is read for the sake of teaching, so that Abraham's honor is not thought to be affected.
The story of Tamar and Judah is read and translated.
Asks why this obvious case needs stating, and what concern might arise.
It is stated so that the reader sees it as praise for Judah.
The first account of the golden calf is read and translated.
Asks why this needs stating, and what concern might arise.
It is stated because the calf episode was followed by atonement, so it is all the more to Israel's credit.
The curses and blessings are read and translated.
Asks why this needs stating, and what concern might arise.
The concern is that the congregation would be discouraged, so the text is stated plainly.
Warnings and penalties are read and translated.
Asks why this needs stating, and what concern might arise.
The concern is that people might observe the commandments only out of fear.
The story of Amnon and Tamar, and of Absalom, are read and translated.
Asks why this needs stating, and what concern might arise.
It is stated so as not to read David's honor as affected.
The story of the concubine in Gibeah is read and translated.
Asks why this needs stating, and what concern might arise.
It is stated so that Benjamin's honor is not thought to be affected.
The Ezekiel passage about making known Jerusalem's abominations is read and translated.
Stated to exclude the view of R. Eliezer, which is then illustrated by an anecdote.
Anecdote of a man who read the Ezekiel passage before R. Eliezer and was rebuked, and was then found to be illegitimate.
Mnemonic list of the passages read but not translated, beginning with the incident of Reuben.
R. Hanina b. Gamliel in Kabul asks the translator to translate only the latter part of Genesis 35:22, and the sages praise him.
The second account of the calf is read but not translated.
Asks which portion of the calf narrative is the second account.
The second account runs from And Moses said until And Moses saw.
Baraita: one must be careful in wording answers, since Aaron's answer to Moses gave the heretics a pretext to deny God.
The priestly blessing is read but not translated.
Asks the reason.
Because the blessing contains the words may He bless and keep you, which is read without translation.
The accounts of David and Amnon are read but not translated.
Asks how this fits with the earlier statement that the Amnon and Tamar account is read and translated.
No contradiction: the earlier view refers to Amnon son of David, and the later to Amnon alone.
Baraita: disgraceful words in Scripture are read in softer terms, with examples, and R. Joshua b. Korha explains the term for idolatry.
Rav Nahman: all mockery is forbidden except mockery of idolatry, supported by Isaiah 46.
R. Yannai derives from Hosea 10:5 that one should read kevodo as kevido, a burden, when speaking of an idol.
R. Huna b. Manoah, citing R. Aha, permits an Israelite to tell a gentile to take away his idol, and Ashi permits disgracing someone with bad reports.
Closing formula of the chapter, introducing the next Mishnah.
Mishnah: a town that sells its square may buy a synagogue, and a synagogue sold may buy an ark, and an ark sold may buy covers for scrolls.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: if they sold covers they may buy scrolls, but a sold Torah may not be replaced by lesser items, and the same applies to surplus money.
Gemara opens with the case of townspeople who sold the town square.
Rabbah b. Bar Hanah in R. Yohanan's name: this is R. Menahem b. Yose's view, while the Sages hold the square has no sanctity.
Asks what R. Menahem b. Yose's reason is.
People pray there on fast days and at gatherings, so it has sanctity; the Sages hold this is only occasional.
R. Yonatan, via Samuel b. Nahmani: the rule that a synagogue may be sold applies only to village synagogues, not town ones.
Ashi: the synagogue at Matha Mehasya may be sold, since people come to it only at his discretion.
Objection from R. Judah: a Jerusalem synagogue of the coppersmiths was sold to R. Eliezer and used for his own purposes, though it was in a large town.
That was a very small synagogue, which the sellers had built themselves.
Objection: a verse on leprosy in the house of your possession implies houses are defiled, while Jerusalem is not, and R. Judah's statement is then reconsidered.
Asks on what point the two Tannaim disagree.
The first Tanna holds Jerusalem was not apportioned to the tribes, while R. Judah holds it was, as a tannaitic dispute shows.
Baraita: the portions of Judah and Benjamin in Jerusalem, with the Temple Mount and the chambers in Judah's share.
A strip of Judah's land ran into Benjamin's portion, where the altar was built, and Benjamin therefore hosts the Shekhinah.
Following Tanna: houses in Jerusalem may not be rented because they do not belong to anyone, and the host seized the hides of sacrifices forcibly.
Abaye: the case teaches that a man should leave his empty wine flask and skin rug at his guest house.
Rava: the rule applies only where the seven good men of the town sold the synagogue without the assembly; if they sold it in assembly, the sale stands.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A sale stands even if the buyer intends to drink liquor in the building.
Ravina has a synagogue mound and asks whether seed may be planted on it.
Asks whether the mound may be sown.
Ashi: buy it from the seven good men of the town in the assembly of the townspeople, and then sow it.
Rami b. Abba wants to dismantle an old synagogue to build a new one, and R. Papa and R. Huna both forbid it, following R. Hisda.
Rava: an old synagogue may be exchanged or sold for secular use, but may not be rented or pledged, since its holiness remains.
Asks the reason for that distinction.
Because the holiness remains in the building itself.
The bricks of an old synagogue may be exchanged or sold but not lent; new bricks raise no objection.
Even on the view that mere intention has legal force, that applies only to a shroud, whereas these materials are not yet fixed for that use.
R. Aha and Ravina disagree about whether a synagogue given as a gift keeps its sanctity.
The one who permits holds the giver would not have given it without benefit, so the gift amounts to a sale.
Baraita: accessories of a mitzvah may be discarded when worn out, while accessories of holiness must be stored in a geniza, and examples of each are given.
Rava: he first thought a stand for a Torah scroll was an accessory of an accessory, but seeing the scroll placed on it, he judged it holy.
Rava: he first thought a curtain was an accessory of an accessory, but once it was folded and a scroll placed on it, it became holy.
Rava: a worn ark may be made into a smaller ark but not a stand, and a worn curtain may become a mantle for a whole scroll but not a single humash.
Rava: bags for humashim and boxes for scrolls are holy accessories and must be stored in a geniza.
Asks why this is needed, since it seems obvious.
These were used for protection rather than out of respect for the scrolls, so the rule is stated to cover them.
A Roman Jews' synagogue opened into a room with a corpse, and Rava says the wooden ark placed there does not transmit defilement.
Objection: sometimes the ark is moved with a scroll on it, making it movable when full and empty, so the ruling cannot hold.
Mar Zutra: worn covers of scrolls may serve as shrouds for a met mitzvah, which is their genizah.
Rava: a worn Torah scroll should be buried beside a scholar, and Aha b. Jacob says it should be put in an earthen vessel, citing Jeremiah 32:14.
Rav Papi and Papa report Rava's ruling on turning a synagogue into a study hall, while Aha reports the opposite ruling.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Papi's view is more reasonable, since R. Joshua b. Levi permits turning a synagogue into a study house.
Bar Kappara's derashah on the burning of the house of God, with R. Yohanan and R. Joshua b. Levi giving two readings of the great house.
Each reading rests on a verse: the Torah view on Isaiah 42:21, the prayer view on Elisha's great deeds in II Kings 8:4.
Infers that R. Joshua b. Levi is the author of the Torah reading, since he permitted turning a synagogue into a study house.
Mishnah: when they sell a Torah they may not buy scrolls of other books.
Asks whether one may sell an old Torah scroll to buy a new one, when the new one adds no higher sanctity.
Come and hear: the Mishnah allows buying a Torah with the proceeds of a Torah sale, so the rule is only against buying other scrolls.
The Mishnah speaks of the case after the fact, whereas the question concerns what is permitted ab initio.
Baraita: a Torah scroll may be wrapped in the covers of a humash, but prophets and writings may not be wrapped in a humash cover.
Objection: the baraita's wording cannot establish the answer, so no conclusion follows about covers of one Torah scroll in another.
Baraita: one Torah may be placed upon another, and a Torah on humashim, but not prophets and writings on humashim.
Placing one item on another differs from wrapping because it cannot be avoided, as in rolling scrolls; so it is permitted.
Baraita from R. Shimon b. Gamliel: one should not sell an old Torah to buy a new one with the proceeds.
That ruling is about the risk of neglect, while here the new scroll is already written and awaiting payment.
R. Meir: one should sell a Torah scroll only to study Torah or to marry, from which one infers that exchanging a Torah for another is permitted.
Study is different because it leads to practice, and marriage is permitted as Isaiah shows, but selling one Torah for another is not.
Tannaitic teaching: one should not sell a Torah even if he does not need it; Rabban Shimon b. Gamliel adds that selling it to feed oneself brings no blessing.
Rava: the restriction applies only where money was left over from a sale; surplus from a collection may be used freely.
Abaye objects: if the case is a sale with surplus, the stipulation would make no difference.
Explains that the case is about a sale with surplus only when no stipulation was made by the seven good men in assembly; with stipulation they may use it even for a dukhsusya.
Abaye asks a student who recited a mishnah before R. Sheshet whether he heard from R. Sheshet what a dukhsusya is.
The student replies that R. Sheshet defined it as the town horseman.
Abaye: a student who hears a term he does not understand should ask someone often with the Rabbis, since such a person has surely heard the answer.
R. Yohanan in the name of R. Meir: people who move to another town and are assessed there should pay, and bring the money back to aid their own town's poor.
Baraita with the same rule: the group pays and brings the money back, while an individual's assessment goes to the poor of the town he is in.
R. Huna proclaims a fast; R. Hana b. Hanilai and the men of his town ask for the charity they gave back so they can support their own poor.
R. Huna replies, citing the teaching that the rule applies only where there is no town scholar in charge.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continuation: a town scholar in charge of charity takes priority, all the more so for personal funds.
The Mishnah rules communal property may not be sold to an individual, per R. Meir, since sanctity is lowered.
Objectors say R. Meir's logic would also bar selling from a large town to a small one.
The Gemara answers for R. Meir: sanctity from a town persists, so only communal-to-individual sales lose it.
Sages argue the same concern applies to sales from a large town to a small town.
They cite Proverbs on the king's glory lying in the multitude as support for the concern.
R. Meir: a synagogue may be sold only on condition that it can be reclaimed.
The sages: it may be sold permanently, except for four uses such as bathhouse or tannery.
R. Judah: it may be sold for use as a courtyard, and the buyer may do as he pleases.
Asks how people could live in the synagogue under R. Meir's view, since the rent would be interest.
Yohanan explains R. Meir follows R. Judah's view that contingent interest is permitted.
A baraita on a loan secured by a field, with differing rulings on who takes the produce, supports this.
R. Judah says that even if the buyer takes the produce, it is permitted.
Judah cites an incident involving Baitus b. Zunin as evidence for his view.
Objectors say the incident proves nothing, because the seller and not the buyer took the produce.
Asks what the disagreement between the authorities is actually about.
The dispute is over contingent interest: one authority permits it, the other forbids it.
Rava says all agree that contingent interest is forbidden.
Rava clarifies the real dispute concerns interest taken on condition of returning it.
The sages' view restated: the synagogue may be sold permanently.
Shmuel rules that one may urinate within four cubits of a place of prayer.
Joseph asks what new teaching this is, since it was already learned.
Joseph's point is supported by citing the Mishnah's ruling on R. Judah's view.
The rabbis' restriction applies only to a synagogue whose sanctity is permanent, not to adjoining areas.
A tanna taught before Rav Nahman the rule about praying and urinating, four cubits apart.
The objector accepts one half of the rule but challenges the reverse case.
Support from a mishnah on how far one must distance oneself from urine and excrement.
Reductio: such a rule would make all the streets of Nehardea sanctified.
Proposes that the text should be taught differently, with a waiting period instead.
Asks why one who has prayed must wait the time to walk four cubits before urinating.
Ashi explains that the one who prayed still has his prayer in his mouth and lips.
A mnemonic word list for the rules just discussed.
Disciples ask Zakai how he lived so long.
Zakai lists his practices, including never urinating near prayer and never skipping Kiddush.
A teaching: his grandmother left three hundred barrels of wine, and he left his sons three thousand.
Huna is found standing before Rav girded with a string.
Rav asks what the string is.
Huna explains he pawned his girdle to obtain wine for Kiddush.
Rav blesses Huna that he be smothered in silk robes.
At Rabbah's wedding relatives throw silks on Huna until he is smothered, and Rav is angry.
Rav asks why Huna did not return the blessing.
Disciples ask Elazar b. Shammua how he lived so long.
He never took a shortcut through a synagogue, stepped on holy people, or lifted his hands without a blessing.
Disciples ask Peridah how he lived such a long life.
No one ever came to the study hall before him.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues a self-description list: never ate meat from an animal whose priestly dues were not taken.
Cites R. Yohanan's ruling that eating meat from an animal with untaken priestly dues is forbidden.
R. Yitzchak adds that such meat is like untithed produce, though the halakhah does not follow him.
Asks whether not blessing before a kohen should count as a praiseworthy trait.
Objects that R. Yohanan's ruling on a sage blessed before by others seems to contradict the claim.
Answers that the ruling refers only to equals, so no conflict arises.
Disciples ask Nehunia b. Hakaneh how he lived so long.
Nehunia lists his traits: no honor from a friend's shame, no curse on his bed, generosity with money.
He never sought respect through a friend's humiliation, illustrated by R. Huna and the spade.
Illustrated by Mar Zutra forgiving all who troubled him, and by Job's generosity with his money.
Akiva asks R. Nehunia how he lived so long.
Narrates that the attendants beat Akiva, who then sat atop a date tree.
Akiva asks why Numbers says a lamb and also one, challenging Nehunia's reading.
Nehunia tells the attendants to leave Akiva alone, since he is a rabbinical student.
Nehunia explains that the word one means unique in its flock.
He never accepted gifts or insisted on retribution, and was generous with his money.
Illustrates refusing gifts with R. Elazar, who declined the Patriarch's gifts and invitations.
R. Elazar quotes Proverbs that he who hates gifts shall live, as justification.
Zera likewise refused the Exilarch's gifts but attended his invitations to honor him.
Nehunia says he did not insist on retribution for his own grievances.
Rava teaches that one who waives his right to retribution has all his sins waived.
Supported by Micah's verse that God pardons sins and passes over transgression.
Rabbi asks R. Joshua b. Korha how he lived such a long life.
Joshua deflects with a jest; Rabbi replies that this is Torah and he needs to learn.
Joshua says he has never looked at the countenance of a wicked man.
R. Yohanan rules that it is forbidden to look at the image of a wicked person.
Supported by II Kings: Elisha looks at Jehoshaphat's presence only out of regard for him.
R. Elazar: Isaac's eyes dimmed because he looked at the wicked Esau.
Objects that the cause may instead be Abimelech's curse of Sarah, which R. Yitzchak treats as fulfilled.
Both causes contributed to the dimming of Isaac's eyes.
Rava derives the lesson from Proverbs: it is not good to favor the face of the wicked.
On his deathbed Rabbi asks Joshua for a blessing, and Joshua wishes him half his days.
Rabbi asks whether the blessing excludes the full length of days.
Joshua replies that otherwise those who come after would have to graze cattle.
Abuha and Minyamin each state a self-praise: never looking at a non-Jew, never partnering with one.
Disciples ask R. Zera how he lived such a long life.
Zera lists his traits, including not sleeping in the study hall and never rejoicing in a friend's downfall.
Mishnah: Judah rules a ruined synagogue may not be used for eulogies, ropes, nets, drying produce or shortcuts.
Supported by Leviticus: the sanctity of desolate sanctuaries remains, so their holiness persists.
Grass growing in a ruined synagogue should not be plucked, to avoid causing grief.
A baraita: synagogues must not be treated lightly, so one may not eat or drink in them.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: synagogues may not be used for adornment, strolling, shelter from sun or rain, or private eulogy, but may be used for study and public eulogy
R. Judah: the rule applies while the synagogue is in use; once ruined, grass may grow and should not be pulled, to avoid distress
Objects that grass is not mentioned in the Mishnah, so the baraita text must be missing a clause
The corrected baraita: synagogues should be swept and the floor beaten so grass does not grow in them
R. Judah's ruling repeated: grass may grow in a ruined synagogue and should not be plucked out of distress
Assi: Babylonian synagogues were built on condition, so people still do not treat them frivolously
Asks what exactly the frivolous conduct is
Frivolous conduct means doing business calculations inside a synagogue, as Assi explained
Assi adds that a corpse may be left overnight in a synagogue where calculations are done
Objects that this cannot be meant literally, since leaving a corpse overnight there would be absurd
Explains the ruling as referring to a corpse of a mitzvah left there in the end
Restates the Mishnah: one does not adorn oneself in synagogues
Rava: sages and their disciples are exempt from the adornment prohibition
Supports Rava by R. Yehoshua b. Levi, who reads Bei Rabbanan as the house of the rabbis
Restates the Mishnah: one does not enter synagogues to escape sun or rain
Illustrative story: Ravina and R. Ada b. Matana entered a synagogue during rain to continue their learning
Aha b. Rava asks R. Ashi how a person should summon someone out of a synagogue
R. Ashi: call by the appropriate scholarly means, such as halakhah, Mishnah or a verse, or else wait briefly and rise
Mishnah clause: public eulogies may be delivered in synagogues
Asks what a public eulogy actually looks like
Examples: a eulogy where a particular scholar is present, shown by Hisda and Sheshet in turn
Rafram eulogized his daughter-in-law in the synagogue for his own honor and the dead's, drawing everyone
R. Zera eulogized a rabbinical student in the synagogue, with a similar self-referential remark
Resh Lakish eulogized a student who taught halakhot to many rows, lamenting the loss to the Land of Israel
Rav Nahman was asked to eulogize a man who knew Sifra, Sifre and Tosefta and replied with a wry image
Remark contrasting the rigorous scholars of the Land of Israel with the saints of Babylon
Cites a Mishnah about one who makes use of the crown of Torah
Resh Lakish explains that the warning applies to one who takes service from someone who repeats halakhot
Ulla: one may accept service from one who repeats the four orders of Mishnah but not from one who teaches them
Story: Resh Lakish crossing water was carried on the shoulders of a man who had learned the Mishnah
Resh Lakish asks the carrier whether he can read Scripture
The carrier replies that he can read Scripture and recite the four orders of Mishnah
Resh Lakish rebukes him that his four rocks of learning do not justify carrying a great man, and throws him into the water
The carrier replies he would rather teach Resh Lakish something than be rebuked
He teaches a statement of R. Zera: women were so stringent that they waited seven clean days even for a spot of blood
Baraita from the house of Eliyahu: whoever repeats halakhot is assured of the world to come
Supports this by a verse from Habakkuk, reading halikhot as halakhot
Opening formula of the next baraita, cut off at the end of this daf

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: Torah study may be suspended for escorting a dead body and for bringing a bride into marriage
Report that R. Judah b. Ila'i used to suspend Torah study for these two duties
Qualification of the Mishnah: suspension applies only when there are not enough people present for the task
Asks how many people count as sufficient
Rav, via Shmuel b. Inia: twelve thousand men, with six thousand of them carrying trumpets, by one version
Ulla: enough people to form a procession from the burial ground to the town gate
Sheshet: removal of Torah study must match its giving, so it takes sixty myriads, but only for readers of Scripture and Mishnah
Baraita of R. Shimon b. Yohai: Israel is so beloved that the Shekhinah goes with them into every exile
The Shekhinah accompanied Israel into Egyptian exile
Supports this from the verse where God revealed Himself to the house of Eli's father in Egypt
The Shekhinah accompanied Israel into Babylonian exile
Supports this from Isaiah, where God says he sent Babylon for Israel's sake
The Shekhinah will also accompany Israel when they are redeemed in the future
Supports this from Deuteronomy, where the verb shav is read as God returning along with them
The exegesis shows that God returns with Israel from all the exiles
Asks where in Babylonia the Shekhinah dwells
Abaye: it dwells in the synagogue of Huzal and in the rebuilt synagogue of Nehardea, alternating between them
Abaye vows to pray in any synagogue within a parasang, since the Shekhinah is there
Anecdote: Shmuel's father and Levi sat in the Nehardea synagogue and heard the Shekhinah arrive, so they rose and left
Story: Sheshet stayed seated in the Nehardea synagogue when the Shekhinah came, and the ministering angels were alarmed
Sheshet asks God who is to yield to whom between the lowly and the one who is not lowly
God replies that Sheshet should be left alone
Ezekiel: God was a little sanctuary to the exiles, cited as the basis for what follows
R. Yitzchak: this refers to the synagogues and study houses of Babylonia
Elazar: this refers to the house of our teacher in Babylonia
Rava's exposition of Psalms 90:1 as referring to synagogues and study houses
Abaye's own practice: he studied at home and prayed in synagogues until he learned from David that he should study there
Baraita of R. Elazar HaKappar: Babylonian synagogues will in future be transplanted to the Land of Israel
Supports this from Jeremiah on Tabor and Carmel, and draws an a fortiori inference about synagogues
Bar Kappara's exposition begins by citing Psalms 68:17 on mountains
Bar Kappara's reading: a heavenly voice rebukes the mountains for challenging Sinai, which is free of blemish
Compares the word gavnunim in Psalms with gibben in Leviticus 21:20 to support the reading
Ashi: from this we learn that an arrogant man has a blemish
Ruling: one may not use the path as a shortcut
Asks what a kapandria, a shortcut, is
Rava: the term is self-explanatory, meaning cutting across the building instead of going around it
Abahu: if a path was there originally, using it is permitted
Nahman b. Yitzchak: one who enters without intending a shortcut may later use it as one
R. Helbo in the name of R. Huna: one who enters a synagogue to pray may later use it as a shortcut
Supports Helbo from Ezekiel 46:9 about entering by the north gate and leaving by the south
Mishnah: if grass grew in the cemetery plot, one should not pluck it, to avoid distress
Objects with a baraita: one may not pluck grass to feed animals, but may pluck and leave it, which conflicts with the Mishnah
Replies that our Mishnah also teaches plucking and feeding, so the baraita is not contrary
Baraita: one should not act disrespectfully in a cemetery, nor graze animals or run water through it, and burn gathered grass on the spot
Asks which clause the burning-on-the-spot rule applies to, since it seems to show no respect for the dead
Rather, the rule refers to the first clauses of the baraita
Mishnah: the reading order for the special Shabbatot in Adar, Nisan and the rest of the year
Gemara cites a Mishnah in another place: on the first of Adar a proclamation is made about the shekels

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah clause: the proclamation also covers the laws of diverse seeds, kilayim
Asks why the shekel portion is announced on Adar 1, since kilayim makes sense only at sowing time
R. Tabi in the name of R. Yoshiah: the verse on the new moon offering shows the Torah wants fresh contributions brought
Because Nisan requires fresh contributions, the reading is moved up to the first of Adar so shekels reach the Temple in time
Asks which view this follows, since it would not follow Rabban Shimon b. Gamliel's two-week rule
Cites a baraita: Rabban Shimon b. Gamliel says Passover laws are asked about two weeks before Passover
Even Rabban Shimon b. Gamliel fits, since the tables for the provinces and the Temple are set up on fixed dates
Asks what the portion of Shekalim is
Rav: the portion begins with Numbers 28:2, Command the children of Israel and say to them my offering
Shmuel: the portion begins with Exodus 30:12, When you take the census, Ki Tisa
Explains that Shmuel's view makes sense because shekels are written in that portion
Objects that on Rav's view no shekel material appears in the portion, so what is the reason
Reply: the reason is R. Tabi's view, which links the portion to the offerings
Explains that the Command reading makes sense because sacrifices are written there, as R. Tabi holds
Objects that on the Ki Tisa reading sacrifices are not written, but socket shekels are
Cites R. Joseph's baraita on three separate contributions: for the altar, for the sockets, and for Temple repair
On the Ki Tisa reading, the Rosh Hodesh is distinguished from other new moons
Asks what distinguishes this Rosh Hodesh on the Command reading
On other new moons six read the day's portion and one the new moon, but on this one all read the new moon portion
This works if the portions follow the regular order of readings
Asks what distinguishes this Rosh Hodesh if the haftarah follows the order and the regular portion is read
Other new moons have six reading the day's portion and one the new moon, but here three and four
Objects with a baraita: when Rosh Hodesh Adar falls on Shabbat they read Ki Tisa and the haftarah of Yehoyada
On the Ki Tisa reading the haftarah fits, since it has the phrase about the money of the persons
Asks what similarity the haftarah has on the Command reading
It is similar, as R. Tabi said
Objects with a baraita: if Rosh Hodesh Adar falls on a neighbouring portion, it is read and repeated
On the Ki Tisa reading, the portion falls about that time, so the case fits
Asks whether the Command portion ever falls at that time
Yes, for the people of Eretz Yisrael, who complete the Torah reading in three years
Cites a baraita in agreement with Shmuel: Ki Tisa is read and the haftarah of Yehoyada
R. Yitzchak Nafha: when Rosh Hodesh Adar falls on Shabbat, three scrolls are taken out, including one for Ki Tisa
R. Yitzchak Nafha: when Rosh Hodesh Tevet falls on Shabbat, three scrolls are read, including one for Hanukkah
Explains that both rulings are needed, because one alone might be read as limited to its own case
Asks why the one ruling does not imply the other
Introduces the dispute over Rosh Hodesh Tevet falling on a weekday
R. Yitzchak: three read Rosh Hodesh and one Hanukkah; R. Dimi of Haifa reverses the assignment
R. Mani: R. Yitzchak Nafha's view is more reasonable, since the frequent takes precedence over the infrequent
R. Abin: R. Dimi's view is preferable, since the fourth reader is needed for Rosh Hodesh
Asks what the practical upshot of the dispute is
Rav Yosef: disregard Rosh Hodesh; Rabbah: disregard Hanukkah; halakhah disregards Hanukkah, with Rosh Hodesh primary
Introduces a case where Shabbat Shekalim falls on the Va'etah Tetzaveh portion
R. Yitzchak Nafha: six read from Va'etah Tetzaveh to Ki Tisa and one from Ki Tisa to And you shall make
Abaye's view on this case, cut off at the end of this daf

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara remark: people might say the Mishnah's stopping point is this one
Abaye's ruling: six read from And you shall command to And you shall make, and one repeats from When you count
Objects with a baraita: if Shabbat Shekalim falls on a neighbouring portion, before or after, it is read and repeated
The baraita works for Abaye but poses a difficulty for R. Yitzchak Nafha
Counter-objection: the baraita fits Abaye only with the Shabbat before, not after, so how can it be read
Abaye's reply: the portion is read on two consecutive Shabbatot, and the same applies here
R. Yitzchak Nafha: when it falls on the When you count portion itself, six read to And Moses assembled and one repeats
Abaye objects that this would mean reading backwards, which is absurd
Abaye's corrected ruling: six read to And Moses assembled, and one repeats from When you count
Baraita in agreement with Abaye: when it falls on the When you take portion itself, it is read and repeated
Mishnah: if it falls in the middle of the week, the reading is moved up to the previous Shabbat
Introduces the case of Rosh Hodesh Adar falling on Friday
Rav holds the reading is moved earlier, Shmuel holds it is delayed
Rav's reason: otherwise too few days remain for the tables to be set up in the provinces
Shmuel's reply: the fifteenth falls on Friday night, so tables would not be out until Sunday, so the reading is delayed
Mishnah: if it falls during the week, the reading is moved up and the special order paused for the next Shabbat
Asks whether the rule applies only to the middle of the week, not to a Friday
Baraita: the first Shabbat is one in which Rosh Hodesh Adar falls within the week, even on Friday
Asks whether Friday should count as the middle of the week, so that the reading is moved earlier
Shmuel's correction: the reading should say on it, as a Tanna of his school also taught
Tannaitic dispute on whether special Shabbatot are interrupted; R. Shimon b. Elazar restricts the rule to a Friday
Cites the Mishnah's second-Shabbat portion, Zakhor
Rav holds Parshat Zakhor is read on the Shabbat before Purim on Friday; Shmuel holds the Shabbat after
Rav's reason: so that the celebration of Purim not precede the remembrance of Amalek
Shmuel replies that walled cities celebrate on the fifteenth, so celebration and remembrance coincide anyway
Objects that the Mishnah's second Shabbat Zakhor conflicts with a case where Purim falls on Friday
Rav Papa: the second means the second Shabbat after the interruption
Baraita: the second Shabbat is one in which Purim falls within the week, even on Friday
Asks whether Friday should count as the middle of the week for the second-Shabbat rule
Shmuel's correction: the reading should say on it, as a Tanna of his school also taught
If Purim falls on Shabbat itself, R. Huna says all agree Zakhor is not read the Shabbat before; R. Nahman says a dispute remains
R. Hiyya b. Abba, citing R. Abba from Rav: if Purim falls on Shabbat, Zakhor is read that Shabbat, before the holiday
Baraita: the third Shabbat is the one after Purim, the portion of the red heifer
R. Hama b. Hanina: the third Shabbat is the Shabbat before Rosh Hodesh Nisan
Reconciles the two views: one refers to Rosh Hodesh Nisan falling on Shabbat, the other to it falling mid-week
Fourth reading: This month shall be for you, Exodus 12:2
Baraita on Rosh Hodesh Adar falling on Shabbat: first Shabbat is Ki Tisa with the Yehoyada haftarah, the second Zakhor
Second Shabbat: Zakhor, with the haftarah from Samuel about the sparing of Amalek
Second-Shabbat rule when Purim falls within the week, or on Friday; third Shabbat is the red heifer
Haftarah for the red heifer Shabbat: Ezekiel 36:25, And I will sprinkle clean water upon you
Third Shabbat: the one after Purim, as above
Fourth Shabbat, This month, with the haftarah from Ezekiel 45:18, cut off at the end of this daf

ranges.en: Baraita: the fourth Shabbat is the one just before the week in which Rosh Hodesh Nisan falls, even if on Friday
Mishnah: on the fifth Shabbat the regular order is resumed
Asks what the regular order means
R. Ammi: the regular order refers to the sequence of weekly Torah portions
R. Yirmiyah: the regular order refers to the sequence of haftarot
Abaye sides with R. Ammi
Supports this from a Mishnah listing the occasions that interrupt the regular reading
Objects to R. Yirmiyah: if haftarot resume the order, there would be a haftarah on weekdays, which does not exist
Reply: each rule holds where it applies, and the weekday case is handled differently
Objects that on fast days the regular reading should not be interrupted, but read in the morning and at minchah, which supports R. Huna
Asks what the practice should be in fact
Abaye: mornings are for the town's affairs; from midday, a quarter of the day is for the Torah reading and the rest for prayers for mercy
Supports the quarter-day division from Nehemiah 9:3, reading the Torah and confessing for a fourth of the day each
Asks whether the order could be reversed, with the Torah reading in the afternoon instead
Rejects the reversal by citing Ezra 9:4-5, where the afternoon sacrifice marks the end of the fast
Mishnah on festival readings: Pesah, Shavuot, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and the days of Sukkot
Mishnah continues: readings for Hanukkah, Purim, Rosh Hodesh, the maamadot and fast days

ranges.en: Mishnah: the blessings and curses in Leviticus are not interrupted; one reader reads them all
Mishnah: on Monday, Thursday and Shabbat afternoon the regular order is read, and these do not count toward the next Shabbat
Supports this from Leviticus 23:44 that each festival is read at its appointed time
Baraita: on Pesah read the festival section, with haftarah from Gilgal, and on the second day from Josiah's Pesah
Cites II Kings 23:22 about Josiah's Pesah as the basis for the second-day haftarah
Asks what the readings of the intermediate days of Pesah are
R. Papa: the readings are summarised by the mnemonic MAPU
Readings for the last day of Pesah and the next day: Exodus 13-15, II Samuel 22, Deuteronomy 15, Isaiah 10
Abaye: communities nowadays read the passages on the ox, the money, the wilderness and the firstborn
Shavuot: Seven weeks, with haftarot from Habakkuk or Ezekiel; with two days, both are read in reverse order
Rosh Hashanah: On the seventh month, with haftarah from Jeremiah 31, or Sarah with Hannah's story
Rosh Hashanah with two days: the second day reads Abraham's testing, with the Ephraim haftarah
Yom Kippur: After the death at morning, forbidden relations at minchah, with the book of Jonah
R. Yohanan: wherever God's might appears, so does His humility, as the Torah, Prophets and Writings each show
Cites Deuteronomy 10:17, Isaiah 57:15 and Psalms 68:5-6, each with the humility clause that follows
First day of Sukkot: the festival section with Zechariah 14 as haftarah, and the two-day practice for the next day
Asks what the haftarah is for the second day of Sukkot
Answer: I Kings 8:2, And all the men of Israel assembled unto King Solomon
Last day of the festival: the firstling passage with I Kings 8:54-9:1; next day Deuteronomy 33 with I Kings 8:22-53
R. Huna in the name of Rav: a Shabbat on the intermediate days reads Exodus 33:12 and haftarah Ezekiel 37 for Pesah and Ezekiel 38 for Sukkot
Hanukkah: the chieftains section, with haftarah from Zechariah 2:14 and I Kings 7:40 when two Shabbatot fall in it
Purim reads Amalek, and Rosh Hodesh reads the new-moon offerings of Numbers 28
Haftarot when Rosh Hodesh falls on Shabbat (Isaiah 66) or on Sunday, the day before (I Samuel 20:18)
Introduces Rav Huna's further ruling, cut off at the end of this daf
